text:
ROUND XVI
AS THEY ARE
A CITIZEN'S DAMNATION OF THE MIDDLEMEN IN THE GULF, AND A CONDEMNATION OF THE ROYAL HOUSES THAT LET THEM IN

Raised by a citizen of the United States under the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence, and laid before the President and the Congress in exercise of the right "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances"

AGAINST the middlemen in the Gulf: the British and French states, damned in Rounds VII and III; the European Union's Commission and agencies, charged in Rounds I and IX; the banks and bureaus that answer to no nation; and the networks that rent the region's free zones.

AND, in condemnation, the seven ruling houses of the Gulf and the five emirates beside them, for the doors they opened and for their record against Americans.

Not against the peoples of the Gulf. Not against the sovereignty of any house. Sovereignty is the point.

I. THE RULE

Our own strategy, November 2025: "The world's fundamental political unit is and will remain the nation-state." It stands "against the sovereignty-sapping incursions of the most intrusive transnational organizations." Of the Gulf, it ends "America's misguided experiment with hectoring these nations—especially the Gulf monarchies—into abandoning their traditions and historic forms of government," and accepts "the region, its leaders, and its nations as they are."

As they are: absolute monarchies on the trade routes of the world. An absolute monarchy is worth one thing to a sovereign republic: a sovereign it can deal with directly, state to state. Without absolute control, it is of no use to anyone. The rule holds for every capital: two signatures where it can be done, and never a signature that is not a state's.

II. YOUR OWN SIGNATURE

Your rulers signed your founding laws. You will be judged by them.

Saudi Arabia, Basic Law, Art. 44: "The King shall be the point of reference for all these authorities."
Kuwait, Art. 1: "There shall be no surrender of its sovereignty."
Bahrain, Art. 1: "Its sovereignty shall not be ceded."
Qatar, Art. 1: "Qatar is an independent sovereign Arab State."
The UAE, Art. 4: "The UAE may not cede its sovereignty."
Oman, Basic Statute, Art. 1: an "independent state with full sovereignty."

In 1776 we charged a king with combining "with others to subject us to a jurisdiction foreign to our constitution, and unacknowledged by our laws." You did it to your own.

III. WHAT WE SIGNED

21 September 1833, Muscat: Edmund Roberts and Said bin Sultan. "There shall be a perpetual peace." Two signatures, fifty-nine years before London's Exclusive Agreements; replaced at Salalah in 1958, again by two. 14 February 1945, the USS Quincy: Roosevelt and Ibn Saud. Two men. No third.

Investment paper with all six, 1975 to 1992: the footing of our Development Finance Corporation. Free trade agreements with Bahrain and Oman; trade frameworks with four.

22 October 2025: Doha and Washington wrote together to Europe's heads of state, around the Commission. 17 November 2025: Riyadh and Washington settled motor-vehicle standards between themselves, after Riyadh had drifted toward Geneva's. That is the template.

We kept faith. This is what was done with the space between us.

IV. THE MIDDLEMEN

LONDON. The first middleman, and by force. 1819: your navy shelled Ras Al Khaimah. Then the treaties of 1820, 1853 and 1892, the last binding the rulers to deal with no power but you. You held their foreign relations until 1971, and replaced rulers who displeased you: Abu Dhabi, 1966; Muscat, 1970. In 1968 you left the Gulf over our objection and banked what we stayed to guard (Round VII). Al-Yamamah: your fraud office dropped it in 2006 after your Prime Minister intervened; BAE pleaded guilty in our court in 2010 and paid $400 million. 2008: Qatari money saved Barclays for the City; your fraud office called £322 million in side fees a fraud, charged the bank and five of its men, and convicted no one.

PARIS. 26 May 2009, Abu Dhabi: opening your base, you pledged to help defend a house's security, sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence, and signed a pact on its internal security. The Louvre's name, leased to a house since 2007. A 2008 tax amendment sparing Qatar's state capital-gains tax on French property. Gulf money landing in fourteen African states as CFA francs rests on your Treasury's guarantee. Your state lender sits beside the EBRD in a house's flagship plants in Uzbekistan.

BRUSSELS. 28 September 2026: Eurojust signed a working arrangement with Abu Dhabi's ministry of justice. Eighteen days earlier your Commission asked to open talks on full agreements with the UAE and seven states of our hemisphere, Canada among them: a house's courts and our hemisphere, in one document. Your Council agreed on 29 October. Your gatekeepers listed the UAE for money laundering in 2023 and delisted it in 2025. Qatargate: members of your Parliament charged over money alleged to come from Doha, which Doha denies.

THE BANKS AND BUREAUS. Riyadh's, Abu Dhabi's and Kuwait's central banks hold shares in Basel (Round IV), whose hub built mBridge with Beijing and the UAE's central bank. Davos (Round X) met in Riyadh in 2024. The Fund: in October, $18.3 billion of Riyadh's, Kuwait's and Doha's deposits sat at Egypt's central bank, assured to the IMF until its programme ends on 15 December 2026, except as equity, and filed in the Fund's own multilateral column. A house's word to a sovereign, rewritten as a bureau's.

THE NETWORKS. No house, sovereign fund or Gulf state body is on Washington's, London's or Brussels' sanctions lists. Their free zones are: 768 entries on our Treasury's list carry an Emirati address, Iran's networks first; 203 on London's, most Russia's; 41 on Brussels'. The RSF kept a financial adviser and proxy companies in Dubai (UN Panel of Experts, 2024). In 2019 the UAE recorded 80,986 kilograms of gold from Mali; Mali declared 567 (UNODC). Islamic Relief: funded by Brussels and London, seated at the UN. London reviewed the Brotherhood in 2015 and declined to ban it.

IRAN. The artery through all of it. This year it fired on every one of you, and on our people in your bases. On 11 March the Security Council condemned it, 13 to none, in Resolution 2817, tabled by Bahrain. Moscow and Beijing abstained.

V. THE HOUSES, AND THEIR RECORD

From our own records and the United Nations'. Your nationals are not your state: a count stands only on the state's own conduct, with what cuts against it beside it.

You have replaced weak hands yourselves: Riyadh, 1964; Doha, 1972 and 1995. You know what a ruler is for.

AL SAUD. Your throne does not run to the Prophet. It runs to the USS Quincy. In August, at Mecca, you signed with Islamabad and Ankara to carry your own defence, as our strategy asks, and our President welcomed it; then you wrote a NATO member into it and barred the exit for ten years. If your war reaches Turkish soil, it reaches Article 5.
1. 1967, 1973. Oil held back from us, then "a total embargo on oil exports to the United States."
2. 1972–80. American-owned Aramco, taken by stages; the first quarter paid at about twice book value.
3. 1988. Chinese CSS-2 missiles, bought "unknown to us." Our ambassador, objecting, was left "no alternative" but to leave.
4. 2000–01. Fifteen of the nineteen hijackers were your nationals. The 9/11 Commission: "no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded" al Qaeda; our Joint Inquiry: some hijackers "received support or assistance from, individuals who may be connected to the Saudi Government."
5. 2001–08. You "failed to impose criminal punishment on any high-profile donor." Our Treasury, 2008: "Saudi Arabia today remains the location from which more money is going to terror groups and the Taliban."
6. 2008. Your official textbooks, taught in Virginia by "an arm of the Saudi government," still carried "overt exhortations to violence" (USCIRF).
7. 2015–25. Cited for not returning abducted American children. Ten are still not home.
8. 2014–15. A royal's office paid a Twitter insider for data on critics. Convicted in 2022 as your agent; one count later reversed on venue.
9. 2016–20. Your consulate paid $100,000 to free the student who killed Fallon Smart, the prosecutor said; he fled. The FBI: "Saudi Officials Almost Certainly Assist Saudi Citizens Flee the United States."
10. 2017–21. Walid Fitaihi, an American doctor, held without charge; his family, "all of whom are U.S. citizens," barred from leaving.
11. 2018. Jamal Khashoggi, a US resident and Post columnist, killed in your Istanbul consulate. Our intelligence: the Crown Prince "approved an operation in Istanbul, Turkey to capture or kill" him. You reject it.
12. 2022. Saad Almadi, seventy-two, of Florida: sixteen years for fourteen tweets.
13. 2022. An OPEC+ cut with Moscow, over our objection that "there was no market basis." You called that "not based on facts."

AL NAHYAN. A founder of mBridge. A member of BRICS. Since 6 October 2026, party to a trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union: five states, with a commission over them. Your services and investment pact with Moscow, 7 August 2025, carried two signatures. The rule is the same for Moscow as for Brussels: the state, never its commission. You banned the Brotherhood and listed Islamic Relief in 2014, then invited in the prosecutors of Brussels, which has funded it.
1. 1973. Abu Dhabi "announced or threatened a total embargo" on us.
2. 1990–2010. "Nuclear traffickers shipped via the UAE because the UAE lacked significant export control laws" (House, 2010).
3. 1997–2001. You recognised the Taliban and stayed one of its "only travel and financial outlets."
4. 1999. Bin Ladin, at a hunting camp beside "an official aircraft of the United Arab Emirates." No strike, for fear of killing a prince. A week after we raised it with Muhammad bin Zayid, the camp was "hurriedly dismantled." He denied officials were there.
5. 2000–01. Nine hijackers transited Dubai; the money moved through UAE accounts; one hijacker "received a salary from the UAE military." The Commission found no evidence of foreign-government funding.
6. 2012. The US-funded National Democratic Institute shut; its American director briefly barred from leaving.
7. 2013. Shezanne Cassim, an American, jailed nine months over a parody video.
8. 2016–19. Raven: former US intelligence operatives hacked for you, into US computers (Justice Department); deferred prosecution, 2021.
9. 2015–19. US weapons passed to Yemeni militias (CNN). Our CENTCOM commander: "We have not authorized Saudi Arabia or the Emirates to retransfer any of this equipment." You deny it.
10. 2019–20. A Pantsir to Haftar under a UN arms embargo (UN panel); you "may provide some financing" for Wagner (DIA). You deny it.
11. 2021. A Chinese facility at Khalifa Port, halted under our pressure: "we stopped the work."
12. 2022–23. Treasury's "country of focus" for Russia-sanctions evasion.
13. 2023–26. Flights from Abu Dhabi to the RSF: "credible" to the UN panel in 2024, unconfirmed in 2025. Treasury sanctioned seven RSF companies in the UAE. You deny arming either side.

AL MAKTOUM. Your free zones are the address book of other men's sanctions, and the gold scale of the Sahel. The fronts register with you. The proxies bank with you. The gold weighs in with you.
1. 1990s–2003. A Dubai firm was "a front for the proliferation activities of the A.Q. Khan network" (President Bush); no US document finds your officials complicit.
2. 2011. Noor Bank, part-owned by your government and chaired by the ruler's son, carried up to 60 percent of Iran's foreign oil sales, US officials estimated.

AL THANI. The open door. Al-Qaradawi preached from Doha for sixty years.
1. 1992–96. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed worked in your Ministry of Electricity and Water. Indicted by us, he escaped: "an official in the government of Qatar probably warned him about it."
2. 2008–15. Al Qaeda financiers designated while living in Qatar. Our Treasury, 2014: "such a permissive terrorist financing environment," a state that had "for many years openly financed Hamas."
3. 2012–24. Hamas's office in Doha. You say Washington asked. A channel was asked for. A home was given. In 2024 we told you its leaders were no longer welcome.
4. 2014. The Huangs, Americans acquitted by your court, held at your airport by a travel ban; our Secretary of State had to call.
5. 2017. For royal hunters held in Iraq, your envoy flew in "hundreds of millions of dollars," seized by Iraq's prime minister as bound for armed groups. You say it went to the Iraqi state.
6. 2020–24. Your state network's American arm, told to register as a foreign agent, had not by 2024.

AL SABAH. Your fund was born in London in 1953, signed with Britain's political agent eight years before your independence: that birth is London's charge. That its office is there still is yours. Since 2025 you levy the minimum tax Paris's tax club wrote.
1. 1967, 1973. You resolved "to stop all oil exports to the United States." The 1973 embargo, decided in Kuwait, reached "refiners supplying U.S. forces in Bahrain, Italy and Greece."
2. 1975–77. Gulf Oil's half of the Kuwait Oil Company, taken by agreement. Aminoil's concession, ended by decree; a tribunal found it lawful, with about $179 million in compensation.
3. 1987. You asked Moscow, too, to escort your tankers. We came.
4. 2008. Your minister called our designation of the Revival of Islamic Heritage Society "unfounded."
5. 2014. "Our ally Kuwait has become the epicenter of fundraising for terrorist groups in Syria" (Treasury). Your new justice minister had "a history of promoting jihad in Syria." He resigned.
6. 2015–16. Your state airline refused an Israeli passenger out of New York, and dropped the route rather than obey our Transportation Department.
7. 2025. On our Treasury's list of states requiring "participation in, or cooperation with, an international boycott."

AL KHALIFA. London's officials put a British officer into your security service in 1966: that is London's charge. You kept him at its head until 1998, twenty-six years after your independence: that is yours.
1. 1973, 1975. An embargo and notice ending our Navy's station, then an order that it leave "by June 30, 1977." The Fleet stayed.
2. 2006. The US National Democratic Institute's director's visa revoked.
3. 2012. American protest observers arrested and deported.
4. 2014. Our Assistant Secretary of State ordered out for meeting the opposition alone. Our Secretary of State called your demand "unacceptable."
5. 2014. A member of our Congress refused a guarantee of entry.
6. 2016. Four American journalists arrested and charged.

AL SAID. Duqm opened to a Chinese industrial park. Thirty-two entries on our Treasury's list carry an Omani address.
1. 1980. With Americans hostage in Tehran: "Oman to give Iraq access to facilities for attack on Iran" (our embassy). Qaboos dropped it.
2. 2016–20. Iran's arms for the Houthis crossed your land and waters; the UN found no evidence of your complicity.
3. 2025–26. The Houthis' "Oman-based spokesman," designated by our Treasury, is in Muscat still. Our embassy has met him there.
4. 2025–26. Bank Muscat, majority state-owned, refuses US remittance services on "unwritten guidance from the Central Bank" (USTR).
5. 2026. In the war, no facilities and no bases for us, your foreign minister said.
6. 2026. Our President: "Nobody is going to control it." Our Treasury Secretary: "Oman, in particular." On 25 August you and Tehran announced "a joint temporary navigational corridor through the Strait of Hormuz."

THE FIVE EMIRATES. 18 December 2025: our Treasury named a ship manager in Sharjah's Hamriyah Free Zone, and four of its tankers, in Iran's shadow fleet. Ras Al Khaimah was shelled into the first middleman's arms in 1819: London's charge.

IN OUR CAPITAL. The middlemen run both ways. From 2001 to 2021 foreign agents filed 148 registrations for principals in Saudi Arabia, 130 for the UAE, 108 for Qatar (Congressional Research Service). In 2025 our universities reported over $1.1 billion from Qatar, more than from any other country. A house that wants two signatures does not rent a third.

Washington has stopped asking you to change. It is asking you to rule.

VI. WHAT WE GAVE

The Quincy, 1945. Escorts for your tankers, 1987 and 1988. Over half a million Americans to free Kuwait and guard Arabia, 1990 and 1991. The Fifth Fleet in Manama. Al Udeid, Al Dhafra, Arifjan. This year our bases on your soil took Iran's fire. On 14 July our President dropped the 20 percent Hormuz fee set the day before and asked the Gulf states for trade and investment deals into the United States instead.

Washington and Moscow drained their treasuries here. We paid in blood. You paid in legitimacy, as sovereign absolute monarchies. What comes next is for the nations involved to settle, not for bureaus and banks in Europe that answer to no nation.

VII. DAMNATION

A navy that shelled its way in and held the rulers' foreign relations until 1971. A fraud case dropped when a Prime Minister intervened. Paris written into a house's defence. A guarantee from Paris under the money of fourteen African states. Prosecutors signed in by working arrangement. Rails laid with Beijing. A house's word to Cairo, filed as a bureau's. Free zones that keep the address book of other men's sanctions. And the houses that opened the doors, with fifty-three counts against Americans on record.

From 1819 to 2026, by their own records, the United Nations' and ours, the middlemen in the Gulf stand damned. The houses that let them in stand condemned under their own founding laws.

There is no reprieve.

THE TERMS I WOULD SET

I hold no office and set no terms. Terms with a foreign power are the President's to set and the Department of State's to carry, and to both I defer. The purse is the Congress's. What touches national security is deferred, without contest. These would be the terms.

I. Off Beijing's rails: Abu Dhabi's central bank out of mBridge. Our strategy rewards those who "align their export controls with ours."
II. Close the arteries: the fronts in your free zones, the ship-to-ship trade in Iran's oil, the registries. Iran's oil and money stop at your ports.
III. Sudan: the RSF's money out of your free zones.
IV. The Brotherhood and Hamas, judged by conduct. A list binds no one. A door does.
V. States, not commissions, in Eurasia as in Brussels: the EAEU agreement replaced by two-signature pacts, state by state.
VI. Cairo: when the Fund's programme ends on 15 December, every Gulf deposit, renewed or converted, goes house to state, out of the multilateral column.
VII. Brussels: no full Eurojust agreement; no European benchmark riding on Gulf money.
VIII. Our own compacts: two signatures from here on. We invited London into Bahrain's compact; that door is ours to close from 20 October 2028.
IX. Standards: ours, set two at a time, as Riyadh did in November 2025.
X. Tether or door. The charters states made, we hold to their text. The banks and bureaus that seat non-state members, or that we never signed, get the door: the EBRD, Basel, Davos. The houses' seats in Basel go with ours. The houses' own institutions are the houses' business.
XI. Our people: Americans held or barred from leaving, freed; abducted children, home; fugitives from our courts, returned.
XII. No shelter: designated financiers prosecuted or surrendered; no home for Hamas or the Houthis' sanctioned spokesman; no Hormuz toll or corridor without us.

To London, Paris and Brussels, and the banks and bureaus beside them: you have been told.
Your exits are already filed: Rounds I, II, III, IV and VII.

THE DOOR
Guidance, respectfully offered to the offices that hold the power this author does not.

No new treaty is needed. Our direct institutions exist: "the International Development Finance Corporation; the Export-Import Bank; and the Millennium Challenge Corporation." The President named the door on 14 July 2026. Two signatures. No third.

THE HINGES
A door that cannot close is not a door. Two signatures opened each of these; either one can close it. The hinges are how the terms are kept. From our own Treaties in Force: 129 entries under the six, 72 read against their texts. Not a recommendation: what the Executive CAN do alone.
ON NOTICE. Air transport, Abu Dhabi (TIAS 02-1211), Doha (20-827), Kuwait (07-527), Muscat (15-116), Manama (13035): a year, the notice sent "simultaneously to the International Civil Aviation Organization" (Art. 15). Even the exit is copied to a bureau. Preclearance, Abu Dhabi (13-1208): twelve months, or one, by us alone, if the UAE falls short of its Art. III. Investment guaranties, Riyadh (8045) and Muscat (8651): six months; cover written survives up to twenty years. Trade frameworks, Riyadh (03-731), Muscat (04-707), Kuwait, Abu Dhabi: six months. Riyadh's National Guard program (7634): six months. Our training mission in Riyadh (8558), and Kuwait's defense procurement and our liaison office (8066): a year. Riyadh's civil technical cooperation (23-508): ninety days.
THE COMPACT WE OPENED. Bahrain (23-1020), London a party since 19 June 2025: no withdrawal before 20 October 2028, then six months (Art. IX). Its implementing arrangements outlive it.
CONGRESS SIGNED THESE. Free trade with Bahrain (Art. 21.5; Pub. L. 109-169) and Oman (Art. 22.5; Pub. L. 109-283): 180 days. Whether a President may withdraw alone is contested ground.
THE SENATE'S SHELF. The Bahrain investment treaty (13065, Art. 16): a year, existing investments protected ten more. The Salalah treaty with Oman (4530, Art. XVI): a year.
KEPT, AND KEPT FOR A REASON. They protect Americans: ICC non-surrender, consular immunities, customs, crime and visa cooperation, Leahy vetting, FATCA, our carriers' tax exemptions, work for our diplomats' families, passage for our Afghan partners, the Peace Corps, our jurisdiction over Riyadh's ships at the Louisiana Offshore Oil Port.
THE DEAD PAPER. Under Kuwait, a 1951 consular convention signed by Washington and London, ratified at London: Kuwait never signed it, and its exit runs between London and us, six months (Art. 29). Under Saudi Arabia, our first agreement with the house, signed in London in 1933, "until the entry in force of a definitive treaty of commerce and navigation." The book lists none. Thirty days, or at once if Congress stops us carrying it out. Under Oman, a science agreement signed at Davos, its term run out on 31 March 2026 unless renewed. Stale or spent: a 1958 Dammam port grant, two F-86 agreements, a paragraph of 1953, and UN Compensation Commission guidelines whose last payment the UN dates to 2022.
THE MULTILATERALS. Three name a house: two wartime declarations, and the Middle East Desalination Research Center, Muscat, 1996, with Israel, Japan, Korea and Oman, open to intergovernmental members: six months (Art. 10(b)).
NOT IN THE BOOK. Four defence cooperation agreements and Riyadh's of November 2025; the 2012 framework with the Gulf Cooperation Council, a bloc, not in force per UNCTAD.
THE PAPER WE CANNOT READ. Ten deferred without contest. Three nuclear: recorded, never offered. Eighteen unpublished. Twenty-six out of open reach.

OUR OWN LEDGER

Two signatures means no invited third and no private third. We built our 2023 security compact with Bahrain open to new members; we and Manama invited London in December 2024. Our own money rides in the middle: Gulf capital in American funds, American giants in the houses' AI ventures, ventures close to our own government. We are the EBRD's largest shareholder, lead the World Bank, whose Rogun group holds four houses' funds, and sit in the Fund that files their deposits as multilateral. Washington: close those doors too.

TO THOSE WHO DO HOLD THE POWER

I make no demand of you. I set beside each office the power it already holds.
The President: the footing, the agreements and the template.
The Congress: the purse, and oversight of every dollar here.
The Treasury: the lists, and the free zones on them.
The Secretary of State: two signatures, house by house, and the air agreements.
The Secretary of Defense: the National Guard program.
The Trade Representative: the free trade agreements and trade frameworks.
The Attorney General: the foreign-agent files.
The Secretary of Education: Section 117.
The Development Finance Corporation: what you back under the investment agreements.

The sixteenth. Read it with all that came before.

We the People

Copying @BIS_org @EBRD @IMFNews @wef @UN @EU_Commission @Eurojust @OECD , so nobody feels left out.

ROUND XVII is loaded.

text:
Softball Recap · Tue., Nov. 10 🥎

Signing Day is tomorrow, and D1Softball just ranked the top 50 incoming Division I classes for 2027, with Georgia Tech's six signees at No. 32.

• Signing Day, Wed., Nov. 11: it is the first day Division I and II athletes can sign a written athletics aid agreement, not a deadline, and schools will announce their signees. Why it matters: no family should feel rushed, so read every line of an offer together first.

• ESPN set the 2027 Shriners Children's Clearwater Invitational (Feb. 18 to 21, Clearwater, Fla.): 11 teams, 27 games on ESPN networks, and national runner-up Texas Tech opens against Clemson on Feb. 18 at 1 p.m. ET. Tickets go on sale Nov. 17 at 1 p.m. ET. Why it matters: spring trip planners have dates now, and the field includes Clemson, Florida State, Texas A&M, South Carolina and Oklahoma State.

• Addison Aleski (@addisonaleski21), class of 2028, 1B/OF with Unity Torres 16U, announced Monday her commitment to play Division I softball at Kent State. Why it matters: 2028s are committing now, but every athlete's fit and pace is her own, so don't measure your daughter against someone else's timeline.

• Top Gun Lone Star Fall Invitational runs Fri., Nov. 13 to Sun., Nov. 15 in Texas with 14U, 16U and 18U divisions. Why it matters: if your team is there, the goal is playing well and enjoying it. Leave coach conversations to email and camps.

Parents tip: Wednesday is the first day to sign, not the last. Read any written offer line by line together. And at weekend tournaments, never approach college coaches in the stands or on the field. A college camp is the only place an athlete talks with coaches on the field.

text:
Global News Brief 
1. Financial Times: Oil prices fell sharply, with Brent crude dropping 3% to $89.21 a barrel, it’s lowest since August, after a 6% decline the previous day. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate fell below $85, while US stock futures rose. Prices remain above prewar levels as the nine-month Iran conflict has restricted Gulf oil exports, raised global fuel costs and contributed to Republican losses in last week’s midterm elections.

2. Reuters: Details of Anthropic’s planned blockbuster IPO, including a proposal to raise nearly $70 billion, were briefly circulated to banks before being withdrawn late Monday.

3. Al Jazeera: Somalia’s former chief justice says more than 300 security personnel occupied the Supreme Court. The allegation comes amid a constitutional crisis after the court ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term extension was unlawful and rejected his dismissal of the chief justice as unconstitutional.

4. The 10-Point: Beef prices could remain high well into the next decade as America’s $100 billion beef industry contracts following years of drought and economic turmoil. The US cattle herd is at its smallest level in 75 years, pushing steak and hamburger prices to record highs. Rebuilding herds takes years, and ranchers, meatpackers and policymakers remain divided over how to address the shortage, leaving few quick solutions for consumers.

5. Wall Street Journal: Wall Street pay is expected to rise this year as market volatility and high-profile IPOs boost firms’ profits, according to Options Group. Last year, the average bonus climbed 6% to a record $246,900, while average total compensation exceeded $561,770, according to New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli.

6. 1440 Daily Digest: A total of 1,156 US public schools closed last academic year, the most since the pandemic, as declining birth rates, falling enrollment and funding pressures strained districts. Enrollment dropped by roughly 1.4 million students between 2019 and 2024, with further declines projected to cut annual state funding by $11.5 billion by 2030–31. Research suggests closures may deliver limited savings while harming displaced students’ academic performance.

7. Financial Times: Nvidia shares closed 4.3% lower on Monday, wiping out more than $192 billion in market value, after its board announced an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese espionage operation. Huang apologized to his family and employees for an affair that US officials believe involved Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed who was allegedly recruited by Chinese intelligence. He pledged to cooperate with the inquiry, led by independent directors and outside lawyers, as the controversy threatens his reputation as a leading figure in the AI industry.

8. 1440 Daily Digest: COP31, the UN’s annual climate summit, opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators from nearly 200 countries, while the US declined to send an official federal delegation for the second consecutive year. Over two weeks, delegates will address emissions pledges, climate-adaptation funding for developing nations and disagreements over transitioning away from fossil fuels. The summit follows the warmest October on record and a third consecutive month above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming benchmark.

9. JPost: House Republicans elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan as their incoming minority leader after Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterm elections. Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, will lead Republicans during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office, replacing Mike Johnson, who declined to seek the leadership role.

10. Florida Press: El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele declared victory in an operation against Haitian gangs, saying Salvadoran forces destroyed the 400 Mawozo gang’s headquarters and its leader’s home. The campaign sparked tensions with US diplomats, who warned that poorly coordinated operations could endanger civilians and other anti-gang forces. The State Department praised El Salvador’s contribution while stressing the need for coordination.

11. Wall Street Journal: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived an impeachment effort after the House voted 211–204 to block it, with Republican votes helping defeat the bid to punish him for his actions as President Trump’s Pentagon chief.

12. Yahoo Finance: Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in early trading Tuesday after a report alleged that a network linked to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy associated with CEO Jensen Huang, helped ship at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia hardware to China since 2023. The allegations intensified concerns over export controls and prompted calls for congressional scrutiny, while the FBI and Nvidia’s board investigate the matter.

13. Yahoo Finance: US stocks declined, with the Nasdaq falling 0.74% to 25,065.88, the S&P 500 dropping 0.38% to 7,520.93, and the Dow slipping 0.30% to 52,231.89. The Russell 2000 lost 0.68%, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.983%. The VIX fell 2.31% to 19.46, gold gained 0.32% to $4,043.10, and bitcoin dropped $1,578.66 to $73,679.12.

text: 4) In politics it is imprudent to take some things for granted. The Republicans did not invest much campaign funds in races in their erstwhile strongholds, many of which their incumbents ended up losing to better prepared Democrats and Independents. Texas, Kansas, Georgia , Mississippi, North & South Carolina, New England... all previously reliable red states all flipped blue in Governor contests, state legislatures and one or both Houses of Congress. The earliest any House can flip back red is 2030. If within these four years Democrats perform well at the local level voters will have no incentive to oust them. Republicans might be looking at a dry spell at both national and state levels comparable to that between FDR and Eisenhower (1933-52).

text:
What makes the Hasbara lies and smears posted and reposted about Ireland's Human Rights review at the UN on Tue morning is that there were so many POSITIVE COMMENTS. Somewhat ironically, given the online smears against Ireland, the item that got the most compliments was our National Action Plan Against Racism 2023-2027 ("NAPAR") which includes, but is not limited to racism that impacts on Travellers, as well as anti-Muslim prejudice and antisemitism. 

Here's some of the POSITIVE FEEDBACK that Ireland received:

Albania
  - Welcomed Ireland's commitments to human rights
  - Commended progress in policing reform
  - Commended progress in combating hate crimes
  - Commended protection of persons with disabilities, incl. ratifying OP-CRPD in 2024

Algeria
  - Commended Ireland's commitment to advancing human rights internationally, notably the right to self-determination and commitment to international humanitarian law
  - Valued efforts to build the national human rights institutional framework, especially measures under NAPAR

Angola
  - Commended continued commitment to human rights through legislative reforms, inclusive policies and strengthened institutions
  - Particularly welcomed NAPAR
  - Welcomed efforts to advance gender equality and disability inclusion
  - Acknowledged constructive engagement with international human rights mechanisms, incl. the CEDAW Committee

Armenia
  - Commended Ireland's steadfast commitment to human rights and its valuable contribution to international cooperation in the field
  - Welcomed efforts to advance gender equality, incl. the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030
  - Highly appreciated sustained investment in children's rights and wellbeing, particularly expanded access to early childhood education and care

Australia
  - Welcomed the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024
  - Welcomed the second National Traveller and Roma Inclusion Strategy
  - Welcomed the review of the Disability Act 2005

Bahamas
  - Commended NAPAR
  - Commended increased investment in affordable housing
  - Commended efforts to expand educational opportunities for disadvantaged children
  - Applauded Ireland's development cooperation, particularly support for education and women's empowerment
  - Applauded Ireland's voluntary contributions to OHCHR
  - Particularly appreciated Ireland's pioneering role as the first donor to the Trust Fund for Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States

Bahrain
  - Appreciated the efforts Ireland has taken to promote and protect human rights

Bangladesh
  - Commended accession to OP-CRPD
  - Commended measures to combat racism and racial discrimination
  - Welcomed initiatives to promote migrant integration and social inclusion
  - Welcomed efforts to prevent human trafficking and protect and support victims

Belarus
  - Welcomed the information on Ireland's implementation of a number of recommendations,
    including Belarus's own from the third cycle

Brazil
  - Commended efforts to strengthen civil society participation in public policy development
  - Welcomed accession to OP-CRPD

Brunei Darussalam
  - Commended continued efforts to advance human rights since the previous review, particularly the National Access Plan 2022-2028
  - Commended adoption of the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030

Bulgaria
  - Highlighted new legislation, stronger national institutions, and strategies and action
    plans in line with recommendations accepted in the third cycle
  - Welcomed the Criminal Justice Act 2024 and its increased penalties for hate-motivated crimes
  - Noted with appreciation that Ireland gives IHREC sufficient human, technical and
    financial resources

Burkina Faso
  - Commended measures taken since the last review to improve the human rights situation
  - Appreciated efforts to ratify OPCAT and set up a national preventive mechanism
  - Noted the Zero Tolerance strategy and measures to combat female genital mutilation

Burundi
  - Commended the Zero Tolerance strategy (cited as being against female genital mutilation)
  - Commended the third anti-trafficking plan and its focus on victims
  - Very much appreciated progress on equality, in particular: the Strategy for Women and Girls; the strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities; initiatives for children's and young people's participation in public life; the youth justice strategy

Canada
  - Pleased with Ireland's accession to OP-CRPD, following recommendations made at the previous review

Chile
  - Appreciated Ireland's efforts in promoting and protecting human rights
  - Highlighted ratification of OP-CRPD, saying it strengthens the international human rights system

Colombia
  - Commended the legislative progress paving the way to ratify OP-CRC and welcomed that the process is underway

Costa Rica
  - Acknowledged Ireland's human rights efforts in protecting children, on migration, and  on non-discrimination

Croatia
  - Commended steps taken since the last review, in particular accession to OP-CRPD in 2024

Cuba
  - Acknowledged Ireland's commitment to the UPR

Cyprus
  - Commended progress since the last review, incl.:
      adoption of NAPAR; increased funding for IHREC; establishment of Cuan; expanded free schoolbooks, school meals and childcare support
  - Referred to "the significant progress achieved"

Czechia
  - Commended Ireland's continued commitment to promoting and protecting human rights

DR Congo
  - Welcomed progress since the last cycle, in particular measures against racism and discrimination through the national action plan
  - Commended efforts to protect vulnerable persons, incl. persons with disabilities and people seeking international protection

Denmark
  - Commended the launch of the National Strategy for Women and Girls
  - Commended progress and additional funding for the National LGBTIQ+ Inclusion Strategy
  - Commended ongoing efforts to remove the three-day waiting period before termination of pregnancy

Djibouti
  - Welcomed Ireland's reforms as showing commitment to its international human rights obligations, incl.:   NAPAR 2023-2027; National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030; National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030

Dominican Republic
  - Recognised Ireland's progress on equality, social inclusion and human rights protection
  - Recognised its commitment to international cooperation

Ecuador
  - Recognised Ireland's accession to OP-CRPD

El Salvador
  - Singled out the extension of funding for pre-school education and care

  - Noted Ireland's efforts to strengthen social inclusion, advance migrant integration and address housing and homelessness, incl. the new Roadmap for Social Inclusion and the comprehensive accommodation strategy

  - Welcomed Ireland's strong commitment to protecting and strengthening human rights

  - Appreciated measures against DSGBV, incl. the third national strategy 2022-2026 and its 2025-2026 implementation plan

Indonesia
  - Commended extending school meals to all primary schools

  - Commended strengthening protection of persons with disabilities
  - Welcomed stronger legislation, incl. the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024

Iraq
  - Valued the efforts made in preparing the national report

Italy
  - Congratulated Ireland on its election to the HRC
  - Welcomed ratification of OP-CRPD
  - Welcomed continued progress on women's rights and gender equality

  - Highly commended progress since the previous review, particularly the national strategies for persons with disabilities and for women and girls

Jordan
  - Appreciated measures to promote the rights of persons with disabilities
  - Noted the third action plan to combat trafficking in persons 2023-2027

Lebanon
  - Valued efforts to promote human rights, equality and social inclusion and to combat discrimination

Luxembourg
  - Welcomed progress since the previous review, in particular the Criminal Justice Act 2024, which consolidates the legal framework against hate crime

Malaysia
  - Commended continued efforts to advance human rights, incl.:  implementation of NAPAR; the new housing and homelessness plan; the Mental Health Act 2026 strengthening rights-based mental health care

Maldives
  - Commended continued efforts to combat racism and promote disability rights, incl.: implementation of NAPAR; accession to OP-CRPD in 2024; the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030

Malta
  - Welcomed Ireland's solid record of ratifying international human rights covenants and optional protocols
  - Highly valued Ireland's level of engagement with the HRC, treaty bodies and other mechanisms
  - Noted positively that the 2024 Hate Offences Act is now in force

Marshall Islands
  - Congratulated Ireland on its election back to the HRC
  - Commended Ireland's legally binding target to cut greenhouse gas emissions 51% by 2030 (vs 2018) under the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act
  - Welcomed the National Dialogue on Climate Action, which engages women, persons with disabilities and local communities

Mauritius
  - Noted positively the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act, which strengthens police performance, accountability and effectiveness
  - Acknowledged increased civil society participation in public policy development

Mexico

text:
The right just lost Congress, and part of the right is cheering. That is the guaranteed way to hell. Pay attention.

Last Tuesday the Democrats took the House and the Senate. Seven Republican Senate seats flipped, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina among them. And a loud part of the right wanted it. They said so for months: let the Republicans lose. Let the Democrats burn it down. Let them hang themselves doing crazy things for two years, and the country runs to a far-right candidate in 2028 and beyond.

That is not strategy. That is volunteering to be the match the other side already wanted.

The election is over. This is now about moving forward. Here is the lesson.

Evil has two sides: the psychotic and the despot.

1. The left is the psychotic, the demonic enemy. It smashes, burns, and murders, and the Democrats drive to hell at 1,000 mph. Nobody here is letting them off. But left against right is only one war. It is the war against the obvious evil. It is the war the ultimate evil uses to keep us distracted while it conquers the world, as it has from the beginning (Ephesians 6:12). None of the "burn it down" men are taking that into account.

2. The deep state is the despot, the ultimate enslavement. It is the orderly devil. Not smash and burn. Absolute control. It is not stupid. It is patient, competent evil that knows no bounds. It uses controlled opposition on the left and on the right. It gets a vote in 2028 and beyond, and it always has. Any plan that leaves it out is either naive or compromised already.

3. The despot wants the fringes raging. It has always used the psychotic to create demand for itself. The psychotic burns. The despot offers to put out the fire. A far left and a far right screaming at each other, which has led to murder and will lead to mass murder, is what it is building. Then it presents a milquetoast Mitt Romney and lets the country flee to him. A far-right candidate to counter a far-left candidate is the matchup it is hoping for. The left already wants its despots to rid the world of the right. The right will offer to do the same with despots of its own: the smash-and-burn rage machine and the total-control despot or king. Either way the despot wins. We must avoid becoming the demonic and our own devil despot.

4. It wants us to discredit ourselves. Nazi salutes. Ridiculous talk. It wants the undisciplined, selfish, feel-good dunks where we shoot ourselves in the foot. Every man who does it on camera works for the other side for free, and we have made that far too easy. Matthew 10:16 was written for men surrounded by wolves. We must be loud, but disciplined. No unforced errors.

5. It kills or arrests those it cannot control. It always has. It strangled and burned William Tyndale in 1536. His crime: putting the Bible in English. Most of the King James New Testament is still his work. It jailed John Bunyan for twelve years. His crime: preaching without the crown's license. He began The Pilgrim's Progress in that cell. Look at Charlie Kirk. Look at JFK.

What wins in 2028 and beyond:

Not a mirror of the far left. A conservative Obama. A palatable, smash-mouth incrementalist who can say the hardest truths like honey, and the female palate will not gag on them. He says things in a way that does not offend, even though it is offensive. That is what Obama did. He won twice, and he was one of the most powerful forces for evil we have ever seen. Imagine that skill in the hands of a righteous man. He speaks to the future young men have to live in: a house they can afford, children they can raise, a country that does not treat them as the enemy.

It is too early to say who the candidate will be. But there are men already showing us what it takes.

James Fishback is 31, the son of a Colombian immigrant, a guy who could be any race. He left Georgetown, built an investment firm, and ran for governor of Florida on what young families cannot afford: a house, the taxes on it, a future. He lost. But he took the college precincts, and his crowds were young men. He showed that young men will show up for a man who speaks to their future.

Joe Kent has integrity and a sympathetic story. Twenty years in the Army, Ranger and Green Beret. Eleven combat deployments. Six Bronze Stars. In 2019 an ISIS suicide bomber in Syria killed his wife Shannon, a Navy cryptologist, and left him with two young sons. He went on to run the National Counterterrorism Center, and in March he resigned it rather than back a war he could not support. He was the highest-ranking official to walk away over it. That is a man who has paid for what he believes.

The standard is integrity plus competence plus the ability to say the hard thing without handing the other side the clip.

What we do here:

Stop amplifying the men who make us easy to dismiss. Every share is a vote for the matchup it wants.

Reward the man who says the hard thing well. Follow him, fund him, and send him to your people.

Stop minimizing the grievances of the young. A man who cannot afford a house or a family is not whining. Hear him and help him. He needs a father, not a dictator.

Look to what Luther got right. He wrote his Small Catechism for fathers to teach at their own tables. We win this around our own kitchen tables, catechizing and discipling our families and neighbors, so that a Christian population creates a Christian nation worth having. This is the way forward for Christian Nationalism.

"A soft tongue will break a bone." Proverbs 25:15. Evil has been patient from the beginning. Now we have to be.

Get ready for Donald's Buyron, Floridumbasses as the @citydelraybeach has just announced they will not host its annual St. Patrick's Day Parade or Pride event in 2027 following the enactment of Florida Senate Bill 1134 (CS/CS/SB 1134), relating to official actions of local governments.

The new state law, which takes effect January 1, 2027, establishes restrictions on municipal funding, promotion, and official actions involving activities defined under the legislation as diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). These restrictions include certain programming and activities designed or implemented with reference to ethnicity, sexual orientation, or gender identity.

Following a review of the legislation and its requirements, the City has determined that it is legally prohibited from organizing, funding, or promoting these events in 2027.

The City recognizes that these annual events have provided opportunities for members of the community to gather, celebrate, and connect. We appreciate the residents, participants, volunteers, and community partners who have contributed to these events over the years.

We remain committed to serving all residents and providing opportunities for community engagement consistent with applicable state and federal laws.

text:
Democrats flipped five governorships—Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada—covering roughly 37% of planned US data-center capacity under the cited estimate, with Texas alone at 22.8%. Incoming governors in Texas, Georgia and Ohio proposed pauses on large facilities, while local ballot results broadly favored restrictions.
Vistra’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA reached $2.378B versus $1.581B a year earlier, and EPS of $3.01 beat the $2.71 consensus. It raised the midpoint of its 2026 EBITDA outlook, with a $7.1–7.5B range, introduced 2027 guidance of $7.7–8.5B and added $1.5B to buybacks. Shares rebounded roughly 10%. Its generation book is 98% hedged for 2027 and 78% for 2028, supporting near-term visibility. Those hedges, however, are not equivalent to data-center supply contracts; unsigned future demand remains exposed.

Restrictions on new construction could increase the scarcity value of existing, energized capacity in suitable locations, supporting a different assessment of $VST and $CEG from leveraged developers. Existing sites and power arrangements also give $MSFT, $AMZN and $GOOGL relative advantages, although slower deployment can delay cloud revenue rather than automatically improve returns. $FSLR and $NEE benefit from policy expectations, with actual orders depending on implementation. Texas already had grid-connection restrictions, so incremental political risk should be assessed separately from existing constraints.

An operating, hedged power asset and a debt-funded project awaiting permits carry very different risks—even when both wear the “AI power” label. Watch how incoming administrations treat new, approved and already-under-construction projects, alongside rules allocating grid costs to large customers. Vistra’s results provide fundamental support, but future earnings still require a close look at contracts, hedge expirations and incremental load. Scarcity alone does not settle the valuation.

text:
The United States does not run a “massive surplus on manufactured goods” with Canada in the sectors now under pressure. The bulk of the trade deficit the U.S. has with Canada is a goods deficit to begin with. A U.S. services surplus helps lower the overall deficit, yet the arrangement is not a balanced agreement by any stretch of the imagination.

Separately, Canada sells 90–95% of its vehicle production into the U.S. market. That dependency, combined with Canada’s own 25% surtaxes on U.S. vehicles, softwood restrictions, and supply-management quotas, is why the current trade actions exist. They are not blanket tariffs on everything Canada sells the U.S. They are targeted at industries the United States can source elsewhere or produce domestically while it continues to take Canadian raw materials.

Canada walked from the USMCA review required under Article 34.7 in August and kept its retaliatory barriers in place. The scheduled rise in U.S. tariffs on Canadian autos and parts to 50% begin on January 1, 2027, is the next step to get Canada to honor its obligations under the USMCA Trade Agreement. 

Manufacturers have already responded: the Jeep Compass is going to Illinois, Stellantis has sold the Brampton plant, and Honda has committed $3 billion to a new Ohio hybrid plant after suspending its large Canadian EV project. These are commercial decisions driven by market size (U.S. GDP roughly $32.5 trillion versus Canada’s $2.3–2.5 trillion) and clearer policy signals south of the border.

“Restoring” USMCA without addressing the trade imbalance does not reverse those shifts. The United States buys roughly 70% of Canadian exports. When the smaller partner outright refuses to negotiate while maintaining barriers, the larger market gets to rebalance its suppliers. That is not the destruction of generational export markets. It is the end of an arrangement in which Canada took reliable, low-tariff U.S. access for granted. The practical step remains returning to the table to reach terms better than the current reciprocal tariffs. We can both agree on that much.

🚨 CFR ELECTION WATCH | MEET JAMES ROSAS: HEARING OFFICER ASSIGNED TO DANIELLE CARTER-WALTERS’ MAYORAL PETITION CHALLENGE!

CHICAGO — November 9, 2026

Chicago mayoral candidate Danielle Carter-Walters began her first day of proceedings before the Chicago Electoral Board following objections to her 2027 mayoral nomination petitions.

Case No. 27-EB-MUN-011 was filed by Patricia Rae Easley, Rickey R. Hendon, and Earl C. Williams, Sr.

Attorney James Rosas is the assigned hearing officer. Carter-Walters has retained legal counsel to represent her during the proceedings.

WHO IS JAMES ROSAS?

Rosas has previously served as a hearing officer in Chicago election disputes involving aldermanic and school board candidates.

In 2023, Rosas handled a petition challenge involving Joseph Mercado, a candidate for alderman of Chicago’s 12th Ward.

Rosas recommended invalidating Mercado’s nomination papers over a required Statement of Economic Interests filing. The Chicago Electoral Board sustained the objection, resulting in Mercado’s exclusion from the ballot.

Rosas was also assigned to the 2023 petition challenge involving former 26th Ward Alderman Roberto Maldonado, who subsequently withdrew his candidacy.

In 2024, Rosas served as hearing officer in a petition challenge involving Felipe “Phil” Luna Jr., a candidate for Chicago’s 7th School Board District.

WHY DOES THIS MATTER?

Hearing officers examine petition challenges, review evidence, and make recommendations concerning whether candidates have complied with Illinois election law.

The Chicago Electoral Board ultimately determines whether to accept those recommendations.

The objections against Carter-Walters include challenges involving petition signatures and her use of a hyphenated married surname.

Monday’s hearing was the beginning of the proceedings, and no final determination has been made regarding Carter-Walters’ nomination papers.

text:
Chase Branham is Indiana’s newest (and first) class of 2027 basketball commit. The 6-4, 185-pound guard from Rogersville, Missouri, officially signed his letter of intent with the Hoosiers on November 11, 2026, under coach Darian DeVries.
He is a consensus 4-star recruit ranked No. 25 by 247Sports, No. 28 by ESPN, and No. 38 by Rivals — making him the 10th-highest-ranked Hoosier recruit in the 247Sports era. He committed in September 2025 over offers that included Purdue, Missouri, Iowa, Tennessee, and others.
High school & AAU background
Branham spent his first three years at Logan-Rogersville High School in Missouri, where as a junior he averaged 21.5 points, 3.6 rebounds, 3.1 assists, and 2.2 steals while shooting 61.7% from the field, 41.1% from three, and 84.8% from the free-throw line. He led the Wildcats to the 2026 Class 4A state title, including a 31-point performance in a semifinal upset of traditional power Vashon. He earned MaxPreps Small-Town All-American honors.
He then transferred to national power La Lumiere School in La Porte, Indiana, for his senior season. On the AAU circuit with KC Run GMC (Under Armour), he posted strong scoring and efficiency numbers, earned All-UAA First Team recognition, and was named MVP of the Under Armour Next City Classic. He also attended USA Basketball Men’s Junior National Team minicamps in both 2025 and 2026.
Scouting profile
Branham is viewed as a dynamic, multi-level playmaker and combo guard who can create on the ball or play off it. He scores efficiently at all three levels, shoots well from deep (including off the dribble), and brings playmaking and defensive disruption. DeVries described him as “a dynamic playmaker that is effective at all three levels” who “continues to push himself to new levels” thanks to his work ethic, while also praising his character.
He is the son of Lori and Nick Branham, has siblings Brooke and Jake, and was born September 5, 2008. He is expected to arrive in Bloomington for the 2027-28 season.

HARRISBURG – On Tuesday, the House Republican Caucus re-elected Rep. Tim O’Neal (R-Washington) to the position of its whip for the 2027-28 Legislative Session.

“It is an honor to be chosen by my peers for the third time to help lead the caucus,” O’Neal said. “House Republicans are committed to ensuring the Commonwealth remains a place of opportunity, where individuals, families and businesses can thrive. We remain dedicated to fiscal discipline, limited government and policies that foster safe, strong and vibrant communities.”

As whip, O’Neal will continue to be responsible for tracking House votes and informing his other 88 Republican colleagues of upcoming issues and legislation.

O’Neal was first elected to the Pennsylvania House of Representatives following a May 2018 special election. In January, he will begin his fifth full term. A life-long resident of southwestern Pennsylvania, O’Neal graduated from Indiana University of Pennsylvania (IUP). While an undergraduate, he served in the ROTC program at IUP and was a member of the Pennsylvania National Guard. After graduation, he served on active duty, including a tour in Afghanistan, rising to the rank of captain. While in combat, he was awarded the Bronze Star with “V” for valor.

Once O’Neal returned from active duty, he settled back in southwestern Pennsylvania and earned his master’s degree in business administration from the University of Pittsburgh’s Katz Graduate School of Business. After working in the energy industry, he was a human resources director for a construction company before his election. O’Neal resides in South Strabane Township with his wife, Julia, and their three children, Lucy, Daniel and Simon.

Joining O’Neal in the House Republican Leadership team for the 2027-28 Legislative Session are:

• Leader: Rep. Jesse Topper (R-Bedford/Fulton).
• Appropriations Chair: Rep. Jamie Barton (R-Berks/Schuylkill).
• Caucus Chairman: Rep. Martina White (R-Philadelphia).
• Caucus Secretary: Rep. Clint Owlett (R-Tioga/Bradford).
• Caucus Administrator: Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence).
• House Republican Policy Committee Chair: Rep. David Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata)

The 48th Legislative District in Washington County covers the city of Washington; Amwell, part of Carroll (Districts 3, 4 and 5), East Finley, Fallowfield, Morris, North Franklin, part of North Strabane (Districts 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), Nottingham, Somerset, South Franklin, South Strabane, and West Finley townships; and the boroughs of Donora, East Washington and Green Hills.

And this has happened not just under the Biden’s insane open border approach, but under Trump’s first term and everyone else before him. 
My opinion:
Should the border be closed like a vault? Absolutely YES!
Should everyone that’s already here go through scrutiny before making a decision? Absolutely YES! 
Should we send back everyone without regards of them embracing the American way of life and smoothly integrating into society after it was the US government who let them in? Absolutely NOT
Should the US easily grant Citizenship to those who came here illegally? Absolutely NOT. They have to Earn It.
But after the scrutiny, grant at least employment authorization, DL (everything in English), and the right to renew them when demonstrating they have complied, and they have integrated, and they are not radicals who came to America but hate it (it’s the government’s job to figure out how, not mine). Make them work for the American dream; that’d be their punishment. That would be a good compromise with a large part of the voters who flipped sides in the midterms. Now, what’s going to be the punishment for those who allowed them in? And what’s the plan to keep the border closed now that Texas is blue or if a democrat enters the White House in 2028 (I hope not)? The republicans need a solid plan or we are all f…d. 
*Keep in mind that they didn’t win Florida by a huge margin. We MUSTN’T LOSE FL!

text:
$ASTS Q3 2026 earnings: AST SpaceMobile's sales almost tripled, but it delayed satellites again

AST SpaceMobile, which builds a satellite network for ordinary smartphones, earned more from government work but delayed its satellites again. Revenue almost tripled from a year ago to $42 million. By our math, the unchanged full-year outlook needs at least $61 million in the fourth quarter, which would be a record.

• Revenue: $𝟰𝟮.𝟯𝗠 (+187% from a year ago; +34% from last quarter)
• Full-year revenue outlook: 𝗨𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 ($150–200M; by our math it needs $61–111M in the fourth quarter)
• Target date for about 45 satellites in orbit: 𝗠𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳 (early 2027 three months ago; 12 in orbit today)
• Debt minus cash: $𝟴𝟱𝟵𝗠 ($249M three months earlier, by our math)

⚖️ 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because AST moved its main satellite target a second time, from early next year to the middle of that year. Paid phone service cannot start at scale before then. The good news: Japan agreed to fund about $1 billion of satellites, and the US Space Force awarded a contract worth about $100 million.

The question now is whether AST can launch enough satellites to start paid service before its cash runs short. Either rockets fly every few weeks from early next year, or the date moves a third time. The launch date for three satellites waiting in Florida will tell first.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲

🟢 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗠𝗶𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀
AST SpaceMobile reports two revenue lines. Products are mainly gateways, the ground equipment that links its satellites to phone networks. Services include milestone payments on US government contracts.

Services did the work. That line tripled from the previous quarter to $21.8 million, while product sales fell 16%. So services passed half of total revenue for the first time this year, at 51.4%.

This matters because government work pays AST before its phone service exists. A new US Space Force sensing contract carries about $100 million of revenue. But customers pay on milestones, so the revenue can jump or drop sharply between quarters.

What to watch: services revenue in the fourth quarter, which AST reports with its annual results. Another quarter near this level would show that the contracts pay steadily.

🟢 𝗝𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗱 $𝟭 𝗕𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀
J-LEO is a satellite constellation that AST plans to build for Japan with its partner Rakuten. Three months ago Japan's communications ministry had made only a preliminary selection.

Now the company reports an agreement that "features approximately $1.0 billion in non-dilutive funding" to make and launch satellites. Non-dilutive means AST issues no new shares for the money. It also listed a pipeline of about $1.2 billion in US quasi-governmental financing for 2027.

That matters because notes and share sales have paid for the build so far. But the release gives no payment dates, and the grant sets a timeline that AST must meet.

What to watch: the first J-LEO cash on the balance sheet. Money received would mean the next satellites need less new borrowing.

🟢 𝗟𝗮𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗵 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘄 𝗖𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟭𝟬𝟬 𝗦𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀
Rockets, not factories, decide how fast AST can deploy. Its Texas plants are already working on BlueBird 51, far ahead of the phone-service satellites it has launched.

This quarter AST said its agreements with "SpaceX, Blue Origin and others" cover over 100 BlueBirds across 2027 and 2028. It also secured a US priority rating under DPAS, the Defense Priorities and Allocations System.

That matters because every launch delay postpones paid service. But a contract reserves a rocket and does not fix a date, and the next flight still has none.

What to watch: launches in the first quarter of 2027, when AST expects a Blue Origin flight and its first DPAS-rated ones. Flights on schedule would show that reserved capacity becomes satellites in orbit.

🐻 𝗕𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲

🔴🔴 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟰𝟱-𝗦𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲
The release says "BlueBirds are on the move". BlueBirds are AST's phone-service satellites, and its deployment plan targets about 45 of them in orbit. The target date moved back instead, for the second time this year.

• Target date at first-quarter results: the end of 2026
• Target date at second-quarter results: early 2027
• Target date now: the middle of 2027
• In orbit today: 12 BlueBirds, none launched since August

The release does not call this a delay. It says three satellites reached Cape Canaveral in September and are "awaiting SpaceX launch date confirmation". Three more should ship by the end of November for a Blue Origin launch.

Chief executive Abel Avellan pointed to the factory instead. "We expect to achieve a production rate of six ASIC satellites per month in December of this year," he said. ASIC is AST's own chip. But a faster factory adds nothing to coverage while finished satellites wait for a rocket.

What to watch: the launch date for the three Florida satellites, and the count in orbit in late March. A count far below the named launches would point to a third move.

🔴 𝗔𝗦𝗧 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗜𝘁𝘀 𝗚𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗕𝗲𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁
Gateways are the ground equipment that links AST's satellites to a phone operator's network. They make up most of its product sales, and until this quarter those sales earned a small profit.

This quarter the hardware cost more than AST charged. Product revenue was $20.6 million, and those products cost $22.5 million.

• Product costs: 109.1% of product revenue, up 17.4 percentage points from last quarter
• A year ago: 71.1%

The loss matters because gateway sales are the revenue AST can earn before phone service starts. Total gross margin still rose to 40.2%, but only because services grew. The release gives no reason for the loss.

What to watch: product costs against product revenue next quarter. A second quarter below cost would mean hardware sales add to AST's cash outflow.

🔴🔴 𝗔𝗦𝗧 𝗡𝗼𝘄 𝗢𝘄𝗲𝘀 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗜𝘁 𝗛𝗼𝗹𝗱𝘀
The release describes a "Fortress balance sheet" with about $3.2 billion of cash. That cash comes from repeated note sales, including $1.15 billion in July. Debt now stands at $4.1 billion, so AST owes more than it holds.

• Debt minus cash: $859 million by our math, up from $249 million three months earlier
• Cash spent on operations and equipment: $464 million in the quarter, by our math
• Interest expense: $30.3 million, above interest income for the first time this year
• Stock-based pay: $52.3 million, more than the quarter's revenue

This matters because AST earns nothing from phone service yet, so borrowed money pays for each satellite. Its operating costs excluding share awards, depreciation and cost of revenues rose 76% from a year ago. The company has now added a rocket programme to its spending plans.

What to watch: debt minus cash at year-end, and whether government money from Japan arrives by then. A gap that keeps widening at this rate would point to more borrowing next year.

🔴 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿
Five standing concerns got no new numbers in the release or the slides. The quarterly filing and the call may answer some of them.

• Contracted revenue: the release does not repeat last quarter's $1.3 billion figure; the filing's contract note will show it.
• The goal of about $1 billion in yearly revenue: AST once tied it to 2027 and gives no date now.
• Paid phone service: no operator pays for service yet; the first service revenue from an operator would move this.
• Ligado spectrum: AST advanced $100 million this year, and the release is silent on approval and on the Inmarsat court case.
• Rivals: AST expects to work with all major US and European operators but names no new contract; rivals such as Starlink pursue the same operators.

👓 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗲𝘀

𝗔𝗦𝗧 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗜𝘁𝘀 𝗢𝘄𝗻 𝗥𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁
AST announced Blacklift, a reusable 20-ton rocket of its own, with launches starting in late 2028. Chief executive Abel Avellan said it should give "greater control over launch availability, deployment schedules, and attractive ownership economics". Each flight would carry up to five BlueBirds, the company's satellites. The release gives no cost, and it lists "proposed transactions with Firefly Aerospace, Inc." and licensed engines among the risks.

𝗕𝗿𝗮𝘇𝗶𝗹 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗔𝗦𝗧'𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲
Brazil granted AST authorisation for commercial service with a combined 50 MHz of spectrum, the radio frequencies its satellites use to reach phones. The company also described a partnership strategy built on spectrum allocations "in markets like Brazil and Colombia". In the US it still targets about 100 MHz, the same goal as last quarter. A licence brings no revenue until satellites cover the country.

— • — • —

💲 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗞𝗣𝗜𝘀

𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀 𝗔 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝘀, 𝘄𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): 𝟯𝟬𝟬.𝟭 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇘ decelerating
The share count is rising more slowly. It grew 10.0% from a year ago. Three quarters earlier the pace was 42.6%. AST funded this quarter with notes instead of new shares, so existing holders gave up less of the company while debt rose.

𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟮𝟲𝟯.𝟯 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇄ reversing
Customer prepayments fell for the first time in a year. Contract liabilities are cash customers have paid for service AST has not yet delivered. They slipped $3.6 million from last quarter, after climbing from $66.6 million a year ago. So no large new prepayment arrived in the quarter.

𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟳𝟵.𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇗ accelerating
Inventory almost tripled in three months, from $28.4 million. It stood at $12.0 million at the start of the year. The release does not say what AST is stocking. That build-up came in the same quarter in which products cost more than they sold for.

𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟭𝟬𝟰.𝟭 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇗ accelerating
Customers owe AST more than it has recorded as revenue all year. Unpaid bills rose 31% in three months to $104.1 million. Nine-month revenue was $88.6 million. The release does not break the balance down, so the reason is not visible yet.

— • — • —

🔮 𝗚𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲

𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟲 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲: $𝟭𝟱𝟬.𝟬–𝟮𝟬𝟬.𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from $150.0–200.0 million
Unchanged. The plan still has revenue at least doubling from last year's $70.9 million, and AST now adds "with upside based on recent contract signatures". By our math, that leaves $61–111 million for the fourth quarter, against $42.3 million this quarter. Even the bottom of that range would be a record. The company has kept this range since it first gave it two quarters ago.

𝗕𝗹𝘂𝗲𝗕𝗶𝗿𝗱 𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝗿𝗯𝗶𝘁: 𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟰𝟱 𝗯𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from About 45 by early 2027
Cut. The date moved back by about a quarter, the second move this year. AST has 12 BlueBirds in orbit, so it needs 33 more by the middle of next year. By our math, the launches it named would bring the fleet to 24 by the end of March. That leaves 21 for the three months after, almost double today's fleet.

𝗡𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘄𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲, 𝗨𝗦 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀: 𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿-𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Start beta service in 2026
Unchanged. AST still plans to switch on service this year in the US, Canada, Japan, Saudi Arabia and the UK. Intermittent means a phone connects only while a satellite passes overhead. An earlier plan put the US step at the end of 2025. The release does not say when operators start paying.

𝗦𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲: 𝗦𝗶𝘅 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵 𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from Six a month by the fourth quarter of 2025
Cut. AST first aimed for this rate a year earlier. It now says two Texas factories run full shifts, and that its own chip goes into every satellite from BlueBird 34. The earlier plan started the chip at BlueBird 50. Six a month equals 18 a quarter, by our math, against three satellites launched in the latest quarter.

𝗕𝗹𝘂𝗲𝗕𝗶𝗿𝗱 𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗱, 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳–𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟴: 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟭𝟬𝟬 𝗶𝗻 𝗮𝗴𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲  ⇗ accelerating
New. AST says its launch agreements now reach a total of over 100 BlueBirds across 2027 and 2028. With 12 in orbit today, that means at least 88 more, by our math. The company gave no split between the two years and no cost for the launches.

— • — • —

❓ 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 $𝟭.𝟯 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗹𝗼𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹?
Last quarter AST added government awards to a figure that used to count only phone operators. The release gives no update. That split shows whether operators have committed more money since late 2025.

𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗹𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝟭𝟮 𝘁𝗼 𝟰𝟱?
The named flights reach 24 satellites by the end of March, by our math. AST has not said which rockets carry the other 21, or when SpaceX will fly the three already in Florida.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗹𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝘀?
AST gave a payload, an engine choice and a first-launch date, but no budget. The answer decides whether $3.2 billion of cash still covers the satellite build.

𝗜𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 $𝟭 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗮 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹?
Management once described a 2027 revenue opportunity approaching $1 billion. With 45 satellites now due in the middle of 2027, a full year of service cannot fit inside that year.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗦𝗧 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗱?
Product costs passed product revenue this quarter, after three quarters of shrinking margins. Readers need to know whether this reflects early units, pricing to win operators, or a one-time charge.

🇺🇸 Progressive Activists Launch “Ready for AOC” Draft Effort as Markets Price Her 2028 Odds at 16 Percent

Progressive organizers have launched a nationwide drive to draft Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, yet Polymarket traders price her chances at just 16 percent while JD Vance holds a commanding lead for the Republican nomination and remains competitive in the general election.

A network of progressive activists announced the “Ready for AOC” effort on Monday, aiming to build grassroots infrastructure that could support a presidential bid by the New York congresswoman. According to The Washington Post and The Hill, the group seeks to recruit 10,000 community leaders across dozens of states and collect one million signatures pledging support, volunteer hours, and votes. Ravi Sahai, a former deputy field director on Zohran Mamdani’s New York mayoral campaign, has described the project as both a demonstration of existing support and a preparatory apparatus should Ocasio-Cortez enter the race. The New York Times first detailed the organizing, which has already enlisted hundreds of local political and labor figures in more than 30 states.

Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a 2028 run for either the presidency or the U.S. Senate. Allies position her as the natural heir to Bernie Sanders’ progressive populist coalition, emphasizing working-class messaging and opposition to concentrated economic power. Yet her record includes sponsorship of the Green New Deal, repeated calls to restructure or abolish ICE, and advocacy for expansive pathways to citizenship. These positions, while energizing a committed base, have drawn sustained criticism for underestimating costs, enforcement realities, and public concern over border control and urban crime. Prediction markets appear to register that tension: Polymarket currently assigns her roughly 16 percent probability of securing the Democratic nomination, trailing Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff.

By contrast, JD Vance enters the same cycle with substantially stronger market positioning. Polymarket prices him near 32 percent for the Republican nomination—well ahead of Marco Rubio and Ron DeSantis—and places him in the top tier of general-election contenders. His background as a Marine, author of a widely read account of Appalachian decline, and current vice president supplies both narrative continuity with the prior administration and a focus on border enforcement, energy production, and cultural traditionalism. Traders appear to view that combination as more transferable to a national electorate than the progressive agenda associated with Ocasio-Cortez.

The “Ready for AOC” launch therefore highlights a structural tension inside the Democratic Party. Midterm gains have emboldened the left flank to press for a candidate whose platform has limited demonstrated appeal outside deep-blue districts. Meanwhile, Vance’s elevated odds suggest that a significant share of capital and attention continues to price a right-leaning nominee as the more plausible vehicle for national victory in 2028. Whether the signature drive alters Ocasio-Cortez’s calculations remains open; the markets currently treat the effort as a sideshow rather than a decisive shift.
