text:
$IRM Q3 2026 earnings: Iron Mountain signs record data center space, but growth cools

Iron Mountain's data centers had their biggest leasing quarter ever, while its fast-growing computer disposal arm slowed. Revenue grew 13% to a third-quarter record, and cash earnings per share climbed 16% to an all-time high. Chief executive Bill Meaney signed a record amount of new data center space and lifted the dividend. The company's own plan now points to about 10% revenue growth in the fourth quarter, the slowest reading this year.

• Sales growth from businesses it owned a year ago: +𝟏𝟐.𝟖% (reported growth 13.5%)
• Cash earnings per share, the measure the dividend is set from: $𝟏.𝟓𝟑 (+16% from a year ago)
• New data center leases signed: 𝟏𝟎𝟐 𝐦𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐬 (13 megawatts a year ago)
• Full-year revenue outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 $𝟏𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (middle of the range: 16% growth)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better, because the data center leases Iron Mountain signed this quarter feed revenue in 2027 and beyond. Its biggest leasing quarter ever and a larger order book point the same way. One caution: growth at the computer disposal arm fell by more than half from last quarter, and the finance chief now plans for about 25% next year on flat part prices.

The question now is whether the computer disposal arm can keep growing without help from component prices. Hytinen said memory prices have stayed level for four quarters, so growth from here has to come from more machines passing through. If volumes deliver, the roughly 25% planned for next year holds; if they do not, the pace slows again. The February figure for that business settles it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐇𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐚 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝟏𝟎𝟐 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐬
Iron Mountain rents space and power to companies that need somewhere to run their computers. A lease pays nothing until the site is switched on, so the leases signed now land in revenue later.

Meaney's team signed 102 megawatts in three months, more than the whole of last year. Two large cloud companies became customers for the first time, and India supplied 74 megawatts of the total.

• New leases signed: 102 megawatts, against 13 a year ago
• Signed so far this year: 137 megawatts, against 63 in all of 2025
• Signed-but-unbilled order book: $575 million
• Data center revenue: $274 million, up 34% from a year ago

Finance chief Barry Hytinen raised the 2027 figure for this business to "$1.3-plus billion", and said "the churn was very low in the most recent quarter". The exposure sits in concentration, because a few cloud buyers take almost all the new capacity, and their pause stalled signings through 2025.

What to watch: how much capacity starts billing, rather than how much gets signed. Iron Mountain switched on 29 megawatts this quarter, and a similar figure in February would show the 2027 step arriving on schedule.

🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐄𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐭𝐨 𝐇𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭
Selling refurbished computer parts lowers Iron Mountain's margin, because those parts carry a cost of goods that rented shelf space does not. That line reached 11.1% of revenue, from 8.5% a year ago.

Two other lines moved the other way. Overheads with sales and marketing fell to 17.5% of revenue from 19.1%, and the labour inside cost of sales fell to 16.1% from 17.3%.

"EBITDA margin was also consistent with the prior year, which is noteworthy given the strong growth in our services revenue that naturally drives a mix headwind," Hytinen said. Profit before interest, tax and depreciation held at 37.6% of sales.

What to watch: the product cost line in February, set against overheads. If both keep moving as they did this quarter, Iron Mountain is trading margin for growth on purpose, and the trade is working.

🟢 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐁𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝟒𝟎% 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
Iron Mountain also sells Insight DXP, software that reads documents, whether on paper or already digital, and turns them into data other systems can use. Governments are buying it, and Meaney pointed to "the 40% increase in government bookings or public sector bookings across the globe".

Three wins show the shape. A Middle Eastern government signed "a multiyear contract with a government for our largest DXP deployment to date", with a rollout planned across 30 agencies. Standard Chartered Bank put the platform into Singapore, replacing older software, and a United States federal customer awarded a three-year records contract worth $25 million.

What to watch: whether digital revenue keeps setting records once these contracts start billing. Iron Mountain publishes no separate line for the division, so the service revenue inside its records business is the proxy, and February brings the next reading.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐈𝐓 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐚𝐥 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝟑𝟖% 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝟖𝟐%
Asset lifecycle management, or ALM, is Iron Mountain's business for collecting old computers, wiping the data and reselling the parts. Its revenue leans on the price of memory chips and on the month a cloud operator strips out a building.

Revenue reached $241 million in the quarter. Growth from a year ago came to 43%, against 88% three months earlier. Hytinen called the result better than planned, helped by enterprise customers, while the part that dismantles cloud computers grew only in low double digits.

• Like-for-like growth: 38%, after 82% last quarter
• Timing: about $30 million of dismantling work moved into the June quarter
• Adding that work back: roughly 60% growth, by our math
• Plan for next year: about 25%, assuming part prices hold

Iron Mountain presents ALM as a share-gain story, and Meaney said "we're not only growing with the market as we're gaining share". Yet Hytinen's plan for next year assumes prices stay put, so a 25% target against a 38% quarter is the firm's own step-down.

What to watch: the fourth-quarter ALM figure in February, which the full-year plan puts near $240 million by our math. A reading near that, with enterprise demand holding, would make this a price story rather than a demand one.

🔴 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬
Iron Mountain funds new data centers and a rising dividend out of cash it has not yet earned. Nine-month operating cash flow of $1.2 billion fell short of what construction and the payout took together, so lenders covered the gap.

• Capital spending, nine months: $1.7 billion
• Dividends paid, nine months: $0.8 billion
• Total borrowings: $18.1 billion, 11% above a year ago, including $1.0 billion of notes due in 2027

The ratio lenders watch sits at 4.8 times earnings, which Hytinen called the lowest since before the 2014 conversion to a property trust. It holds there only because profit compounds, while debt climbs and quarterly interest reached $217 million.

What to watch: the 2027 spending plan, due at the March investor meeting. A programme near this year's $2.2 billion keeps the ratio steady; a larger one on the same payout policy means more borrowing.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing worries got no fresh number this quarter, either because Iron Mountain does not publish the figure or because the next reading is months away.

• Full-year margin: the plan implies 37.1% of revenue before interest, tax and depreciation, under last year's 37.3%
• Physical records: neither storage volume nor the retention rate appears in these materials, and the tape and disk line fell 9%
• Currency: Hytinen put the stronger dollar at "like $5 million, could be as much as $10 million" off fourth-quarter revenue
• Earn-outs from ALM takeovers: the liability reached $210 million, and revaluing it cost $70 million over nine months, outside the cash measures

What to watch: the February accounts and the new segment split. Separate disposal figures, a storage volume number and a fourth-quarter margin near 38% would answer three of these four at once.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐢𝐭 𝐅𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬 𝐌𝐢𝐬𝐬 𝐈𝐫𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐧'𝐬 𝐒𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐬
Several American states are tightening the rules on new data centers. Meaney named Texas, Ohio and Georgia as the most restrictive and added: "We're not developing any sites in those 3 markets." The 325 megawatts Iron Mountain expects to switch on within two years already carries permits and committed power.

𝐒𝐞𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
Iron Mountain reports two segments, records and data centers, with the computer disposal and digital businesses folded into a corporate line. Hytinen said the finance team is "evaluating how we align our segment reporting" and will set out the new shape in February. Investors would then see disposal revenue and profit on their own.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟏𝟒𝟗.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Rent grew 11.3% from a year ago, slower than last quarter's 12.3%, with data centers doing the heavy lifting. Records rent rose 5.4%. Hytinen said that stripping a one-off benefit in last year's tape and disk business lifts that figure above 7%, "this is the highest growth rate the team has delivered on that line in over 2 years".

𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟑𝟎.𝟔%  ⇄ reversing
The tax charge rose to $56.7 million from $16.6 million, after Iron Mountain set aside allowances against foreign tax assets. That cost roughly $0.09 per share of reported earnings by our math. The measure the dividend is set from excludes such items, so cash earnings per share still rose 16%.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟓𝟎𝟕.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Money owed by customers grew 9.9% from a year ago, slower than revenue at 13.5%, which is the direction a landlord wants. Hytinen credited "significantly improved working capital" for part of the cash result. Nine-month operating cash flow of $1.2 billion is the highest the business has recorded.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟑𝟎𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
The count rose 0.7% over the year, as staff share awards vested. Iron Mountain buys back no stock, so shareholder cash leaves entirely as dividends, which came to $790 million over nine months and step up again in January.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: ~$𝟐,𝟎𝟑𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $1,995–2,065 million implied by the August full-year outlook
Unchanged in substance. The plan calls for about 10% growth, the slowest reading of the year and below this quarter's 13%. It falls inside what the August full-year range already implied, by our math. The base explains part of it, because last year's fourth quarter carried a large Chicago lease start and high memory prices.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟕,𝟗𝟓𝟎–𝟖,𝟎𝟐𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from $7,940–8,010 million
Raised. The middle of the range moved up $10 million, leaving growth of about 16% for the year. It is the fourth increase in four quarters, and each is smaller than the last: +$175M, +$100M, +$10M. Hytinen said the new range absorbs a stronger dollar since August.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: ~$𝟕𝟖𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $765–795 million implied by the August full-year outlook
Unchanged in substance. About $780 million implies 11% growth. The margin lands near 38.4% of revenue, which is where the fourth quarter sat last year. It rests on year-end seasonality and on a revenue mix tilting back towards rent as part sales ease.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟐,𝟗𝟒𝟖–𝟐,𝟗𝟕𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from $2,945–2,975 million
Raised. The middle of the range moved up $3 million, which leaves growth of about 15% for the year. By our math the year still ends at 37.1% of revenue before interest, tax and depreciation, a shade under last year, because reselling computer parts carries a cost of goods.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐅𝐅𝐎 (𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬): ~$𝟒𝟕𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $461–481 million implied by the August full-year outlook
Unchanged in substance. Iron Mountain looks for about $473 million of cash earnings, 10% above last year. This is the figure the dividend is set against. The quarter just reported came in $18 million above the August projection, mostly on lower cash interest and taxes.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐅𝐅𝐎 (𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬): $𝟏,𝟕𝟖𝟎–𝟏,𝟖𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from $1,760–1,780 million
Raised. The middle of the range moved up $20 million, to roughly 16% growth. Nine months are done at $1,317 million, so the fourth quarter needs about $473 million. Hytinen named working capital, cash taxes and capitalised interest as the levers behind this year's run of better-than-planned results.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞: ~$𝟏.𝟓𝟕  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from about $1.56 implied by the August full-year outlook
Unchanged in substance. About $1.57 a share means 9% growth, the slowest quarterly rate of the year, because last year's fourth quarter was already strong. The dividend declared for the period takes roughly 63% of that, in line with the policy Iron Mountain states.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐅𝐅𝐎 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞: $𝟓.𝟗𝟒–𝟔.𝟎𝟎  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from $5.87–5.93
Raised. The middle of the range moved up $0.07, to about 15% growth. This is the fourth increase in four quarters, each smaller than the one before: +$0.085, +$0.075, +$0.070. The quarterly dividend rises 15% from January, which matches that rate.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐋𝐌 (𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐚𝐥) 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 $𝟏,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from Approaching $1,000 million
Raised. Hytinen said: "we now project ALM revenue to be modestly ahead of $1 billion for the full year". Nine months brought $761 million. The fourth quarter therefore needs about $240 million by our math, close to the quarter just reported. The plan assumes memory prices stay where they have been for four quarters.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐓 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐚𝐥 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧?
Iron Mountain reports asset lifecycle management inside a corporate bucket and gives only 'solid improvement in contribution'. Investors cannot see whether enterprise work or the lower-margin resale of cloud hardware carries the profit.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐨𝐟 𝐀𝐋𝐌 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬?
Hytinen says memory prices have been flat for four quarters and next year's 25% plan assumes they stay there. The split between price and volume in this year's revenue has never been published.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐝𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧-𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨?
Deferred purchase obligations reached $210 million from $134 million at year-end, and revaluing them cost $70 million over nine months. The maximum payout and the deals behind it are not disclosed.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧?
The presentation calls storage volume a record, but neither the release nor the quarterly filing gives the cubic feet or the retention rate. Both numbers decide whether price increases rest on a stable base.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐬𝐞𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐬𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐭 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐰?
Hytinen says the reporting lines are under review, with an answer in February. Whether ALM and digital get their own revenue and profit lines changes how much of this story investors can check.

text:
ICYMI: President Trump on 60 Minutes: “We Have Historically Good Numbers”

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Last night, President Donald J. Trump sat down with 60 Minutes following the midterm elections and made a powerful case for his America First record. President Trump highlighted the booming Trump economy 165,000 new jobs in October, record 401(k) balances, and hundreds of billions of dollars in new factories touted the most secure border in history, detailed the decisive blows he has dealt to Iran’s nuclear program, explained why America must win the Super Intelligence race, and much more.

Key exchanges:
• On the midterms: “I think if I was on the ballot, it would’ve been a much different situation…But there’s something beyond that. They didn’t like the war. They didn’t like the fact that gasoline went up…And there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.”

• On the stock market: “We have historically good numbers. We have the highest stock market in history.”
• Since President Trump was elected, the S&P 500 has hit 77 new record highs, the Nasdaq has hit 70 record highs, and the Dow has hit 51 record highs. Since Inauguration Day, the S&P 500 has hit 67 record highs, the Nasdaq has hit 60 record highs, and the Dow has hit 43 record highs.

• On jobs numbers: “The numbers are way beyond anybody’s expectations… We had 165,000 jobs created just in a short time.”
• The U.S. economy added 165,000 new jobs in October smashing economists’ expectations; manufacturing added 19,000 jobs in October and the sector has added more than 100,000 jobs since its December 2025 low.

• On retirement savings: “401(k)s are at their all-time high by a lot. Under other Presidents, they were a disaster. 401(k)s have made people rich.”
• 401(k), 403(b), and IRA balances hit new highs in the second quarter of 2026, with the average 401(k) balance reaching a record $155,800 up 13.1% from a year earlier.

• On private investment: “There has never been a time where there is the activity trillions and trillions of dollars right now, as we sit, is being built. In a year from now… many of those plants are gonna be open, operating.”
• Companies are pouring money into America, including Apple ($600 billion and 20,000 new American hires), NVIDIA (up to $500 billion in American-made SI infrastructure), TSMC ($165 billion in the largest single foreign direct investment in U.S. history), and Johnson & Johnson (more than $55 billion).

• On reshoring auto manufacturing: “We’re also building automobile factories like we’ve never built before.”
• Audi is building its first-ever U.S. plant in Georgia, with a $4 billion investment that will create about 4,500 new jobs.

• On reshoring pharmaceutical manufacturing: “How about pharmaceutical? Eli Lilly, Merck, Pfizer they’re building hundreds of billions of [investment].”
• Eli Lilly has committed more than $50 billion to American manufacturing, Merck has committed more than $70 billion, and Pfizer has committed an additional $70 billion as part of its landmark agreement with the Trump Administration to lower drug prices.

• On securing the border: “I think I got an A+ for closing up the border… I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.”
• Border Patrol recorded just 98,708 southwest border apprehensions in FY2026 the lowest in agency history and a 95% drop from the Biden-era average while September marked the 17th straight month of zero releases at the border.

• On Iran: “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon. I think, historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not, but I have to go with what’s right for our country.”

• On the Strait of Hormuz: “The strait is open, Ross… Your favorite newspaper, The Wall Street Journal… had an article that said, ‘There’s more oil going through the Hormuz Strait than there was at the beginning of the war.’ Think of that.”
• The Wall Street Journal reports that Persian Gulf oil exports have surpassed prewar levels more than 24 million barrels a day thanks to a shipping system under U.S. protection.

• On Venezuela: “I just say the Venezuela attack will go down in military histories… It was one of the most incredible attacks anyone’s ever seen. They left the aircraft carriers at 1:00 in the morning, pitch black. Everything went perfect.”

• On the Russia-Ukraine war: “I believe that war is going to end and it’s going to end soon, and the only reason it’s going to end is because of me.”

• On Super Intelligence: “The reason I’m an AI bull, one of the reasons, is because President Xi left here two weeks ago we had a great meeting he’s all-in to SI… Whoever wins that race wins.”

• On data centers: “China has no problem with data centers. China has no problem with electricity. And, by the way, we don’t either because… I’m demanding that they build their own electric plant.”

• On MAGA: “MAGA is basically common sense. MAGA is strong borders, good military we have created wealth at a level that our country has never seen before.”

• On 2028: “We have a tremendous bench.”

• On how his presidency will be remembered: “That I made America great again.”

Distributed on November 9th, 2026.

text:
$HNRG Q3 2026 earnings: Hallador signs record power contracts, but takes on costly debt

Hallador Energy, an Indiana coal and power producer, bounced back from a summer plant outage and locked in its highest electricity prices ever, while taking on expensive debt to build a second power plant. Quarterly sales rose 28% from the second quarter to $130 million as power generation jumped, narrowing the net loss to $4.5 million. In October, chief executive Brent Bilsland signed a multi-year power deal above $80 per megawatt-hour that lifted the total segment backlog to $3.0 billion.

• Total revenue: $𝟏𝟑𝟎.𝟑𝐌 (-11% from a year ago, +28% from last quarter)
• Contracted power backlog: $𝟐.𝟐𝟐𝐁 (+38% from last quarter on October deal)
• Total debt: $𝟓𝟓𝟏.𝟗𝐌 (up from $45.0M after $600M bridge loan)
• Turtle Creek investment decision: 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐞𝐧𝐝 (pushed back from September 2026)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because solving the gas turbine funding crunch came with a steep financing bill that offsets the new power contract. Securing a $600 million bridge loan allowed Hallador to take ownership of its turbines in the Philippines and put $265 million into escrow without selling new shares today. The bad news: the loan requires a minimum repayment of 1.35 times the funded amount even on a refinancing—at least $743 million on the $550 million draw by our math—and outside power purchases hit $11 million despite the planned outage ending.

The question now is whether signing long-term customers for the Turtle Creek gas plant in early 2027 lets Hallador replace the bridge loan and cover the rest of the $800 million budget without issuing heavy equity. If buyers sign up at high capacity rates, project lenders could fund the gap; if talks drag on, paid-in-kind interest and the 1.35 times payoff floor will squeeze shareholders. The final investment decision before year-end and early 2027 contract announcements will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐭𝐨 $𝟐.𝟐 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧
Hallador produces electricity at its Merom coal plant in Indiana and sells both energy and accredited capacity, which is a commitment to have power ready when the grid needs it. In October, the Indiana power producer signed its third major multi-year supply deal of 2026, locking in prices starting in 2029.

• Combined price on the October deal: over $80 per megawatt-hour, the highest in the company's history
• Total contracted power backlog: $2.22 billion, up 38% ($616 million) from last quarter by our math
• Average contracted capacity and energy price: rises from $46.07 per megawatt-hour in 2026 to $75.35 in 2031–2035

This matters because the October contract pairs high-grade energy prices with the capacity deals signed earlier this year. Earlier, the company kept its energy beyond 2028 open to wait for better prices. Getting over $80 per megawatt-hour proves buyers will pay a premium for guaranteed power late in the decade.

What to watch: contracted energy volumes for 2029 and 2030 in the fourth-quarter report. Adding more volume near $50 per megawatt-hour would show the October pricing applies across the rest of the plant's open output.

🟢 𝐆𝐫𝐢𝐝 𝐒𝐭𝐮𝐝𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭
Turtle Creek is Hallador's planned 460-megawatt natural gas power plant next to its existing Indiana station. "MISO notified us that the interconnection study, which ran through MISO’s Expedited Resource Addition Study program, is complete," chief executive Brent Bilsland said, referring to the regional grid operator's fast-track review.

In October, the power producer also took legal ownership of unused gas turbines bought for $350 million in the Philippines and put the remaining $265 million purchase price into escrow. Those turbines are now on a ship to the United States for Siemens to inspect, keeping the second half of 2028 start date within reach.

What to watch: the signed grid interconnection agreement and the upgrade cost bill in the fourth-quarter filing. A manageable grid upgrade bill would clear the way for the board's final investment decision before year-end.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐡𝐞 $𝟔𝟎𝟎 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐁𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐠𝐞 𝐋𝐨𝐚𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐚 𝟏.𝟑𝟓𝐱 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐨𝐟𝐟 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭
Last quarter, Hallador owed $339 million for its gas turbines with only $84 million in liquidity, creating a risk of default or heavy share sales. Management wants to build the gas project and "build value at each development stage with little to no equity dilution", Bilsland said, while expanding the project makes the business attractive and "broadens the group of investors who can own our shares and finance our company".

This quarter, the power producer closed the funding gap by taking out a $600 million senior secured construction bridge loan, drawing $550 million at closing. That cash paid off old bank debt, triggered a $5.7 million debt extinguishment loss, and put $330 million into restricted cash to cover the turbine escrow.

However, the loan terms in the risk disclosures show a steep price. The facility charges paid-in-kind interest, puts liens on almost all assets, and requires "a minimum return of 1.35 times the funded amount payable on any repayment (including a refinancing)". By our math, repaying or refinancing the $550 million draw will cost at least $742.5 million, an extra $192.5 million on a project budgeted at $800 million.

What to watch: the interest rate and maturity schedule of the $600 million bridge loan in the third-quarter 10-Q filing. Those details will show how fast paid-in-kind interest builds toward the 1.35 times repayment floor.

🔴 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐝 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞
When Hallador's coal units break down during hot weather, the utility has to buy replacement electricity on the open market to meet its delivery contracts. In the second quarter, unplanned downtime at Unit 2 pushed purchased power costs up to $8.6 million while Unit 1 sat in a 60-day planned maintenance outage that finished in July.

Power generation jumped 77% from the second quarter to 1.4 million megawatt-hours once Unit 1 returned, cutting maintenance costs by 6.1 percentage points of revenue from a year ago. Yet the cost of purchased power rose again to $11.1 million, or 8.5% of revenue, up 7.1 percentage points from a year ago, while labor rose 4.6 points and overhead rose 2.1 points.

What to watch: unit availability and purchased power expense in the fourth quarter, when no major outage is scheduled. Another quarter above $6 million in outside power purchases would point to ongoing reliability problems on the 1980s coal units.

🔴 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐄𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐚 𝟗𝟎-𝐃𝐚𝐲 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐭
The headline $3.0 billion segment backlog includes $421.5 million of energy sales between 2029 and 2035 from the new October contract. Unlike standard fixed-volume deals, the footnote explains that those figures are management estimates derived from forward power curves.

The contract covers a base load of 200 megawatts, but it is unit-contingent—meaning required volumes drop if a Merom generating unit is offline—and it "permits the counterparty to reduce the base quantity to zero for a maximum of 90 days per year". Because the buyer can turn off deliveries for a quarter of the year when market prices are low, realized sales could fall well below the backlog table.

What to watch: whether future supply contracts for Merom and Turtle Creek give buyers similar 90-day volume options. Relying on flexible volume clauses would make post-2028 cash flows less predictable than fixed capacity payments.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Three standing risks in the business received no resolution in the third-quarter earnings release.

• Indiana regulator approval: the 12-year capacity contract over $1 billion still awaits Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission sign-off, which was targeted on or before November 15, 2026.
• Gas plant customer contracts: Turtle Creek still has no signed buyer agreements, with management now targeting deals with investment-grade customers in early 2027.
• Coal plant rules and outside buyers: third-party coal sales fell 30% from a year ago, and the release gives no update on post-2030 environmental compliance costs at Merom.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐲 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐈𝐧 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖
Across the Midcontinent grid, utilities and data centers face a shortage of power plants that can run on demand rather than only when the wind blows or the sun shines. That scarcity is visible in Hallador's contracted capacity prices, which jump from $244 per megawatt-day in 2026 to $478 in 2029 and $502 in 2030.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 / 𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟏𝟑.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Contract liabilities—cash customers paid upfront in 2024 and 2025 for electricity to be delivered later—fell 23.7% from $149.1 million at the end of 2025, by our math. As Hallador delivers this low-priced power without cash coming in, nine-month operating cash flow was negative $25.1 million. Management says these legacy prepaid deals expire in the second quarter of 2027.

𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝-𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟔.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Sales of coal from Sunrise Coal to outside buyers dropped 29.5% from a year ago and 11.0% from the second quarter. Lower outside coal revenue caused the 11.1% drop in total quarterly company sales, while electric revenue held steady from a year ago at $92.8 million.

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): -$𝟕𝟖.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
By our math, cash burn widened from negative $50.2 million in the second quarter and positive $3.7 million a year ago. Hallador used $21.8 million in operating cash flow while spending $57.1 million on capital projects for the gas turbines and July coal plant upgrades.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐤 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from September 2026
Pushed back by up to three months. The power producer previously targeted September 2026 for both the board's final investment decision and the signed grid connection contract. Although the grid operator finished its study, the final grid contract, construction agreement, and remaining equipment orders are still being completed.

𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐤 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐞: 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐟 𝐨𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Second half of 2028
Unchanged. The company still plans to start running the 460-megawatt gas plant in the second half of 2028, despite the one-month delay in shipping the turbines from the Philippines and the later investment decision. Hitting this date is required under the new $600 million credit agreement to avoid an event of default.

𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐤 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 & 𝐕𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭: $𝟖𝟎𝟎𝐌 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 / ~$𝟏.𝟔𝐁 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from Below $800 million
Unchanged on cost, with a new value target added. "Our goal at Turtle Creek is to seek to roughly double an $800 million investment into $1.6 billion of value over the next 24 months," chief executive Brent Bilsland said. Management added that the $600 million bridge loan and a planned $75 million credit line leave more capital still to be raised.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐝𝐨𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟏.𝟑𝟓𝐱 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐠𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐲?
The $600 million bridge loan requires a minimum repayment of 1.35 times the funded amount ($742.5 million on the $550 million draw) even on a refinancing. Investors need to know the interest rate and whether signing customer contracts lowers that payoff multiple.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 $𝟏𝟏.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟑?
Unit 1 returned from its planned outage in July and power output jumped 77%, yet Hallador spent more on purchased power ($11.1 million) than during the second-quarter outage ($8.6 million). Management did not state whether Unit 2 suffered more unplanned breakdowns.

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐚 𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟏 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥?
Prior disclosures expected Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approval of the 12-year capacity contract on or before November 15, 2026. Only six days before that date, the release footnote still lists the contracts as subject to regulatory approval without giving a status update.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐝𝐨𝐫 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 $𝟐𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐤?

FIVEBBBBBTV SPORTS

OPINION: Why  Will Lose Its Final Three Games
By FIVEBBBBBTV | November 8, 2026

BLOOMINGTON, Ind. — Indiana is still very much alive. At 8-1 overall and 5-1 in the , the Hoosiers control their own path to the Big Ten Championship Game. 
That is exactly why this next stretch is so dangerous.

I am not predicting a collapse because Indiana is bad. I am predicting it because of timing, wear, and the specific opponents left on the schedule. Here is the case for 0-3 to finish the regular season.

The Record So Far
Indiana’s only loss came on Oct. 17 at home to , 19-15.
Since then, the Hoosiers have not lost — but they have not looked dominant either:
•  Oct. 24 at Michigan: W 13-6 in overtime 
•  Oct. 31 vs. Minnesota: W 23-16 in overtime 
Two straight overtime wins. Two straight weeks of extra football. Two straight weeks of surviving instead of imposing their will. That matters heading into November.

Game 1: Saturday, Nov. 14 vs. 
Opponent record: 7-2 overall, 4-2 Big Ten 
This is not a soft landing after the bye week. USC is coming off arguably its biggest win of the season — a 30-18 win over Ohio State. 
That changes the entire dynamic. USC is no longer just talented. USC is confident, battle-tested, and playing for its own  push.
Indiana, meanwhile, has spent the last two games living on the edge. The Hoosiers needed overtime to beat Michigan and Minnesota. Against a USC team averaging 32.4 points per game, Indiana cannot afford another slow start and another fourth-quarter escape. 
Prediction: USC wins in Bloomington

Game 2: Saturday, Nov. 21 at Washington
Opponent record: 5-4 overall, 2-4 Big Ten 
On paper, this looks like the most winnable game left. On the schedule, it is the trap.
Indiana would be traveling across the country to Husky Stadium after an emotional, physical game against USC — win or lose. Washington is coming off a narrow 25-28 loss to , a game that showed the Huskies have not quit despite a difficult season. 
This is the classic November road game: long travel, cold weather, hostile environment, and an opponent with nothing to lose. If Indiana is 8-2 and bruised coming in, or 9-1 and emotionally spent, Washington has every incentive to play spoiler.
Add in the cumulative toll of back-to-back overtime games in late October, plus USC the week before, and this is where depth and legs start to matter more than rankings.
Prediction: Washington wins in Seattle

Game 3: Saturday, Nov. 28 vs. 
Opponent record: 3-6 overall, 2-4 Big Ten 
Yes, Purdue is 3-6. Yes, Indiana is heavily favored on paper. That is precisely why rivalry games are different.
The Old Oaken Bucket is Purdue’s season. If Indiana enters this game at 8-3 after two straight losses, the pressure flips completely. Indiana would be playing not to collapse. Purdue would be playing to ruin Indiana’s season in Bloomington.
Purdue is averaging 29.4 points per game — enough offense to punish a tired defense — while allowing 32.3 points per game, which means this could turn into a shootout rather than a controlled Indiana win. 
In rivalry games, momentum and desperation often beat talent. After two losses, Indiana would have neither.
Prediction: Purdue wins in Bloomington

The Bottom Line
Indiana’s remaining schedule is:
•  Nov. 14: vs. USC
•  Nov. 21: at Washington
•  Nov. 28: vs. Purdue 

I believe the Hoosiers finish 8-4, not because they fell apart overnight, but because they have been surviving for a month — and November does not reward teams that just survive.
USC has the firepower. Washington has the road trap. Purdue has the rivalry.

Tell me I’m wrong. I hope I am.

Screw the Ds.  They're an ignorant bunch of assholes with big mouths making threats that their bank accounts can't cash.  

Iran has not issued formal, enacted state bounties covering President Trump’s entire cabinet. Reported threats and claimed rewards have focused primarily on Trump himself, with some extending to specific officials involved in economic or security pressure on Iran. Details come from U.S. court records, intelligence assessments, Iranian state-linked media, parliamentary statements, and reporting by outlets including CBS News, Reuters, WSJ, Iran International, and MEMRI.⁠ CBS News⁠ Reuters

President Trump
IRGC-linked plots: U.S. prosecutors charged Pakistani national Asif Merchant (convicted in 2026 of terrorism and murder-for-hire) in connection with an IRGC-directed scheme that targeted Trump (among others). Separately, alleged IRGC asset Farhad Shakeri was charged in late 2024 with directing a plan to kill Trump; he remains at large. Intelligence also prompted security adjustments, including a plane switch after a Turkey summit over a reported surface-to-air missile threat. ⁠CBS News

Clerical fatwas and Blood Covenant campaign: After U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear sites in 2025, senior clerics (including Grand Ayatollahs Naser Makarem Shirazi and Hossein Nouri Hamedani) issued fatwas labeling Trump a mohareb (enemy of God). The “Blood Covenant” group (promoted by IRGC-affiliated Fars News) claimed to have raised roughly $40 million for his assassination via a website; independent estimates put actual pledges closer to $10–20 million. A separate mass text campaign in Iran claimed about $25 million in pledges. ⁠Legalclarity ⁠NY Post

Parliamentary proposal: In May 2026, Ebrahim Azizi (chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee) announced a draft bill (“Reciprocal Action by Military and Security Forces of the Islamic Republic”) that would require the government to pay €50 million (roughly $54–58 million depending on exchange rates) to anyone who kills Trump, also naming Netanyahu and the CENTCOM commander. Multiple reports confirm this remains a proposal under review and has not been enacted into law or funded.⁠ Iranintl⁠Factually

Other historical/related claims: A 2020 Iranian MP offered $3 million; a provincial official later announced roughly $1.14 million. Iranian state media aired a video claiming a $10 million bounty on Barron Trump (funding unverified).⁠ Algemeiner

Cabinet members and other officials
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent: Recent Iranian threats (linked to his leadership of sanctions/economic pressure campaigns) prompted his relocation from a Washington-area home to a U.S. military base. An IRGC-affiliated Fars News video (translated by MEMRI, from the “Yahya Movement”) explicitly threatened Bessent and his husband, accusing him of various crimes and warning of action at locations in New York City or South Carolina. No specific cash bounty amount was reported for him. ⁠Memri⁠Reuters

Other current officials: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, and others have also moved into military housing amid broader security concerns. A October 2026 DNI memo to Rubio warned that Iran had “substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel,” with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and elsewhere. No named monetary bounties for specific cabinet members beyond Trump have been widely reported.⁠ Timesofisrael

Historical context: IRGC operatives previously plotted against former officials including John Bolton (a ~$300,000 offer) and Mike Pompeo. Many current moves reflect ongoing retaliation narratives tied to the 2020 Soleimani strike and the 2025–2026 U.S.–Iran conflict.

Iranian officials and media have repeatedly framed these as “reciprocal” or religiously justified responses. Large claimed sums are often unverified pledges, propaganda, or unpassed bills rather than allocated government funds. U.S. authorities treat the threats as serious, leading to protective measures.

🚨 THE REAL STORY NOBODY’S TALKING ABOUT 🚨
This Election Is About Unity, Not Division.

Five Black governors will serve at the same time starting in January. Before this election, only three Black Americans had ever been elected governor in US history, and never two at once. Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman governor in Georgia. Byron Donalds the first Black governor of Florida. Aaron Ford in Nevada. David Crowley in Wisconsin. Wes Moore won reelection in Maryland.
Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman governor in New Mexico. Gina Hinojosa flipped Texas, becoming its first Latina governor and first Democrat there since 1995, beating a three-term incumbent. At least seventeen women will serve as governors in 2027— a record thirty-four percent of all states. Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim US senator. Chris Pappas the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. Democrats now hold a majority of governorships for the first time since before 2010. 

But here’s what the headlines keep missing. 

These aren’t just firsts. They’re messages.

Hinojosa: “I’m not going to be the governor for just Democrats. I’m going to be a governor for all the people of Texas.” People are tired of the divisions, the fighting, the culture wars. This is a time to come together.

Donalds, a Republican: “Even if you didn’t vote for me, you have my word that I will be your governor too.” Not here to represent fifty-one percent. Florida will be a state for everybody.

And the proof is in the pudding. Georgia: two hundred twenty-two million against eleven. Texas: two hundred eighty-one against thirty-seven. Wisconsin: one ninety-five million, sixty percent of it against the winner. North Carolina’s fourteenth: fifty to one and the long shot took it. Tennessee: seven to one, lost. This election wasn’t bought. It was believed.
Same as twenty sixteen. Trump didn’t win on money. He tapped a sentiment the country already had, and anyone who wasn’t a career politician probably would have won that year. It just happened to be him. This cycle proved it again.

It’s not about money. It matters what is said.

Forget the fake news the right is trying to propel about division. 

Listen to what these governors are actually saying. It’s not about parties. It’s about bringing everyone under the umbrella of their governorship.

And now we need to watch for the follow through. Promises are easy on election night. The real test is what happens in January when the cameras leave.

text:
Vance's Veil: The Morning After. 

A vice president does not get to indict the president's war on the morning after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress — the biggest midterm shift since the Reagan years. Seven Senate seats flipped. Governors fell in Georgia and Texas. Whatever the causes, the result was the same: the Republican majority was gone, and Vance chose that exact morning to publish a post of over 600 words indicting the administration he serves. He told the country the war lost the Senate. Then he returned to the White House as if the sentence had no weight. 

That post is the exposure. Not a side note to it. The event itself. Because here's what Vance knew when he hit send, and what the country didn't. His opposition to this war wasn't something he discovered on November 4. It was the oldest thing about him. Why was he the one in the room with Oman's foreign minister before the bombs fell? Why did Iran specifically request him for talks? Why did he refuse to call it a war? 

He spent the year on record saying the president couldn't fire him. Not because he planned to be genuine. Because he planned to perform. Saying it out loud was the rehearsal.

For eight months, two Vances existed. The private one, skeptical from day one. The public one was in the room when Trump ordered the strikes. He sold the ceasefire on television because selling it was the job. His audience during the war was Trump's base, so he performed loyalty. After Democrats seized control, his audience was the 2028 electorate, so he performed honesty. He never left the White House, because that desk is still his. He stacked all three — base, electorate, building — and only dropped the ones that stopped when they stopped paying. He didn't change his mind. He changed his audience. He reads the room before he reads the record. 

The post didn't close that gap. It tore it open in front of everyone — and in doing so, it didn't just reveal the contradiction. It amplified it. Made the disingenuousness impossible to unsee. 

A man who believes his own words resigns. A man who wants the next election clings to power. He did the second and called it honesty. He cannot have both. Not because I say so — because the office won't let him hold both. 

Every day he stays, he embarrasses himself again. The timeline doesn't fade with time — it compounds. November 4 was the exposure. November 5 was the first day of the veil. And it doesn't lift until he takes it off, which means stepping down. Not explaining. Not clarifying. Resigning. Because a man can be caught in a contradiction and walk away. What he can't survive is wearing it like a suit he chose. Vance chose it. He put it on that morning, and he's still wearing it, and every sunrise makes it heavier. The office won't let him hold both, and neither will his own face in the mirror. 

The vice presidency is not a platform for a pollster's four-point list. It is a constitutional office with one job above all others: to be ready to assume the presidency. Vance used that office to distance himself from the man he would replace. That is not succession planning. That is a job application with a government seal on it. 

And the voters who read it know exactly what they saw. Not a statesman. Not a loyalist. A man auditioning for a future that requires the present to fail. 

-- Joseph Fosco 
November 8, 2026

text:
IF I WERE YOU, holding an index fund, a pension or a few shares of the companies building artificial intelligence, I would look at one line in their cash flow statements before I looked at anything else: the line that used to say "repurchases of stock" and now says "proceeds from issuance". The direction of the money has reversed, and nobody sent you a letter.

Big Tech stopped buying its own shares. It started selling them to you. Here is the record, from the companies' own filings, and then the argument. The interpretation is mine and is labelled as such.

THE REVERSAL

For five years the most profitable company in America had one dependable habit. Every quarter, without exception, Alphabet bought back its own shares: about $14 billion a quarter on average, close to $300 billion between 2021 and 2025, more than any other company in the AI race. Thirty-three consecutive quarters, from the end of 2017 to the end of 2025.

First quarter of 2026: zero. Second quarter: zero. Third quarter: zero. The $70 billion authorisation the board approved in April 2025 is still there, $69.5 billion of it unused. Nothing stopped Alphabet from buying. It chose to sell.

On 1 June the company announced an $80 billion equity raise, upsized two days later to $84.75 billion: $20.5 billion of common stock sold to the public at around $355 a share, $10 billion placed privately with Berkshire Hathaway, $19 billion of mandatory convertible preferred paying 6.25%, and a $40 billion at-the-market programme to sell shares over time. The largest equity offering in history, in any industry, beating the $70 billion Petrobras raised in 2010. In the third quarter Alphabet sold a further $12.4 billion through the at-the-market programme and $28.7 billion of bonds. It spent $51.4 billion on property and equipment against $42.3 billion of operating cash flow. Free cash flow: minus $9.1 billion, for the second quarter in a row.

The thesis in one line. The buyback era financed shareholders with cash. The AI era finances capex with shareholders.

EVERYONE EXCEPT MICROSOFT

Alphabet is the cleanest case, not the only one.

Meta spent $44.5 billion on buybacks in 2021, $30.1 billion in 2024 and $26.2 billion in the first nine months of 2025. In the first nine months of 2026: nothing. Third-quarter capex, including finance-lease principal, was $34.9 billion against $32.8 billion of operating cash flow, a negative free cash flow quarter, which, to my knowledge, the company had not reported since its 2012 listing. The 2026 capex guide rose at every release: $115-135 billion in January, $125-145 billion in April, $130-145 billion in July, $135-145 billion in October, which implies $49 to $59 billion in the fourth quarter alone. On 26 October Meta sold $25 billion of common stock through forward sale agreements at $625 a share, five times oversubscribed, plus $12.5 billion of convertible preferred and $1.9 billion more when the underwriters exercised their option; a week later it was back in the bond market. From 19 January 2027 it will distribute a new class of non-voting shares, one for each existing share: a currency it can issue indefinitely without diluting its founder's control, and, according to the offering filing as summarised by TIKR, one it intends to sell to the tune of up to $60 billion from the first quarter of 2027, taking the programme to about $95 billion. Meta's own release lists its funding mix as operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, strategic partnerships and equity capital. Read the list in order.

Oracle bought back $36.6 billion of stock in fiscal 2019 and about $20 billion a year through 2021. In fiscal 2026: $206 million. Capex that year was $55.7 billion against $32 billion of operating cash flow. In February it announced a plan to raise $45 to $50 billion in 2026, half debt and half equity: a $25 billion bond, a $5 billion mandatory convertible at a 6.5% dividend, and a $20 billion at-the-market programme. The stated purpose of the equity: to keep an investment-grade rating while spending.

Amazon, which bought back $6 billion of stock in 2022 and nothing since, and pays no dividend, had little to stop. It borrowed: about $54 billion of bonds in March, after $15 billion in November 2025, and $115 billion of long-term debt over nine months. Third-quarter capex was $77.3 billion, nearly $20 billion above estimates, against $42.4 billion of operating cash flow. Trailing twelve-month free cash flow: minus $42.4 billion, from plus $14.8 billion a year earlier. The 2026 plan is $220 billion, raised from $200 billion in July, and the chief executive says 2027 will be meaningfully more.

Microsoft is the exception, and it is instructive. It still bought back $4.4 billion of stock in the September quarter and paid $6.8 billion in dividends while spending $39.4 billion on plant against $58 billion of operating cash flow. Free cash flow: $18.6 billion. Its CFO says the company stays free-cash-flow positive through fiscal 2027 with capex approaching $170 billion. It is also the only one of the five that has not yet termed out its capex in the long-dated bond market. Microsoft kept the old model because, so far, its cash still covers it. Even so, its buybacks fell from $32.7 billion in fiscal 2022 to $22.3 billion in fiscal 2026.

For a control group, look at Apple, which is not building data centres. Fiscal 2026 buybacks: $86.4 billion. Capex: $9 billion. Operating cash flow: $145 billion. Apple puts 6% of its operating cash into plant and 60% into its own shares. The AI builders have inverted the proportions.

FROM CASH TO DEBT TO EQUITY

The sequence matters, because it tells you where the constraint moved.

Until 2024 the build-out was financed from operating cash flow. The five hyperscalers issued an average of $28 billion of bonds a year between 2020 and 2024, according to Bank of America. In 2025: $121 billion. Oracle's $18 billion in September, Meta's $30 billion in October, the largest non-acquisition high-grade deal ever, Alphabet's $17.5 billion and Amazon's $15 billion in November. In 2026 the dollar issuance of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle and SpaceX passed $180 billion by late October, by TwentyFour Asset Management's count, with Street estimates of $250 billion by year-end and about $400 billion once the wider technology and AI complex is included. Barclays expects total US investment-grade issuance of $2.46 trillion this year and names hyperscaler capex as the main upside risk to that number.

The debt is not only bigger; it is longer. Across 2025 and 2026, 41% of hyperscaler issuance carried maturities beyond 15 years, against 16% for the investment-grade index. Amazon sold dollar bonds due 2076. Alphabet sold a sterling bond due 2126, a century bond, alongside the largest corporate deal ever in Swiss francs and the largest Canadian corporate bond on record. These companies now make up about 4.5% of the US corporate bond index. The 30-year Treasury, at 5.25%, yields about 40 basis points more than at the start of the year, and the supply of 30-year corporate paper competing for the same pension and insurance money is one reason.

Then the constraint moved again. Bloomberg's credit desk reported that the bond market might not absorb all the hyperscalers' needs. Meta's bonds, rated AA-, trade in line with BBB issuers. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps tripled after its September 2025 deal, and in January a group of its bondholders sued, alleging the company had not disclosed how much more it would need to borrow. Keeping an investment-grade rating became the binding constraint, and the answer to that constraint is equity.

So the equity came. Oracle in February: $5 billion of mandatory convertible, $20 billion of at-the-market authority. Alphabet in June: $84.75 billion. SpaceX in June: a $75 billion initial public offering, $85.7 billion with the greenshoe, the largest in history, at $135 a share, followed eleven days later by a $25 billion bond that drew $89 billion of orders and priced about 0.4 percentage points wider than comparable BBB paper. Nvidia, awash in free cash flow, sold $25 billion of bonds the same month, its first in five years. Meta in October: $39.4 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing listings. The supply of AI equity coming to the public in 2027 will be measured in the hundreds of billions.

THE DEBT MATH

Alphabet's total debt passed $100 billion this year, several times what it carried five years ago; it raised more than $85 billion in twelve months across six currencies. At the 5.5% to 7% coupons now prevailing on long-dated hyperscaler paper, each $100 billion of debt costs $5.5 to $7 billion a year in interest, before the preferred dividends. That is affordable for companies earning $25 to $30 billion a quarter. It is also permanent in a way buybacks never were: a buyback can be paused in a bad quarter, as 2026 has proved; a coupon cannot. The order books are still deep, 3.6 to 4.6 times covered at the 30-year point for Oracle, Meta and Alphabet, better than the 3 times average for the investment-grade market. But a market that absorbs $250 billion this year is being asked, on the Street's own estimates, for more than that next year, when group capex passes $1 trillion. The equity raises of 2026 are what happens when a treasurer looks at that number and decides not to find out where the bond market's limit is.

THE TELL IN THE FOOTNOTES

Two details in the filings say more than the headlines.

First, Alphabet's third-quarter report states that the at-the-market programme is primarily intended to meet the tax obligations associated with employee equity grants. For years Alphabet paid those withholding taxes in cash and bought back enough stock to absorb the dilution from stock-based compensation, which ran at $8.6 billion in the third quarter alone. Now it sells new shares to pay the tax, and buys nothing back. The share count, which fell year after year for most of the past decade, is rising. The trend has not paused; it has inverted. Employees are still paid in stock. The cost of that stock has moved from the company's cash to the shareholder's ownership.

Second, the structure of the preferred. Alphabet's mandatory convertible pays 6.25%. Oracle's pays 6.5%. SpaceX's longest bonds yield 6.65%. Those are the coupons of high-yield debt, attached to instruments that convert into the common equity of companies rated AA. When the most creditworthy issuers on earth pay junk coupons for capital that turns into their own shares, the market is telling you how much capital they need and how fast.

WHO IS BUYING, AND AT WHAT PRICE

Alphabet sold common stock to the public at $355.20 on 3 June. The shares closed at $324.89 on 28 October, the day of its third-quarter results, and traded below $293 that evening after the capex figure and the negative free cash flow were digested. SpaceX priced at $135 and fell about 23% from its post-listing high within two weeks. Meta's forward sale was struck at $625; after its results on 21 October the stock had traded around $720. On 5 November, the day after the midterms, the chip and data-centre complex lost roughly $3 trillion of market value on fears that new Democratic governors in Texas, Ohio and Georgia would slow the construction of the very facilities this capital is meant to fund.

Who bought? Berkshire Hathaway took $10 billion of Alphabet, the anchor that made the rest of the book possible. Reports around Meta's sale said Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom, the companies to which Meta's capex is paid, were weighing up to $5 billion of the offering; if confirmed, that is suppliers funding their customer's purchases of their own products, the money loop I described in September, now running through the equity market. The rest was taken by the institutions that always take it: index funds, pension funds, sovereign funds, and through them every household with a retirement account.

That is the transfer this piece is about. In a buyback, the company uses its cash to buy from shareholders who want to leave; the remaining holders own a larger share of a smaller cash pile. In an issuance at the top of a capex cycle, the company sells to new shareholders who want to join; the existing holders own a smaller share of a larger capital base whose return is not yet known. Good or bad depends on one number: whether the return on the new capital exceeds the cost of the equity sold to raise it. A company selling stock at 25 times earnings to build assets that return 17% creates value. A company selling stock at 25 times earnings to build assets that return 6% transfers value from old holders to the build-out, and from the build-out to whoever sold it the chips.

Nobody knows that number yet, and the people selling the shares know that nobody knows it. That is not fraud. It is the definition of selling at the top: the moment when the price reflects the promise and the cash flow has not yet arrived to test it.

A WORKED EXAMPLE, FOR THE HOLDER

Take a company with 100 shares, $100 of earnings and a share price of $25, a multiple of 25 times. It sells 10 new shares at $25 and raises $250. If the $250 earns 17%, the company adds $42.50 of earnings; earnings per share rise from $1.00 to $1.30 and the old holder is better off, even though he owns 9% less of the company. If the $250 earns 6%, the company adds $15 of earnings; earnings per share fall from $1.00 to $1.05 before depreciation and below $1.00 after it, and the old holder has paid for someone else's data centre. The difference between the two cases is the return on the new capital, which nobody will know until the assets have been running for two or three years.

Now add the detail from Alphabet's filing. Suppose the company also pays its staff 2 shares a year and used to buy those 2 shares back with cash. If it stops buying and instead sells 1 more share to pay the tax on the grants, the old holder's dilution is 3 shares a year, not zero, on top of the 10 sold for capex. Over three years that is roughly a fifth of the company transferred to new holders and employees, in exchange for assets whose return is still a forecast.

WHAT THE RETURN LOOKS LIKE SO FAR

Precision, because this is not an argument that the demand is imaginary.

Alphabet's revenue grew 25% in the third quarter to $127.6 billion; Google Cloud's operating income tripled to $11.1 billion; its backlog stood at $467.6 billion at the end of the first quarter, nearly double the year-end figure. AWS grew 39%, the fastest in five years, with a $578 billion backlog. Azure grew 48%, with $678 billion of contracted cloud revenue, though 45% of that backlog in January was tied to one customer, OpenAI, which is still losing money. Oracle's remaining performance obligations reached $523 billion. TwentyFour's analysts note that with a 20-year average return on invested capital of 17.75%, funding at 5.5% to 7% clears the hurdle. The revenue is real. The contracts are real.

Three other things are real. First, capex guidance moved in one direction all year: Alphabet from $175-185 billion to $195-205 billion, Amazon from $200 to $220 billion, Meta from $125 to $140 billion at the midpoint, with 2027 expected to exceed $1 trillion for the group. The only cut, Microsoft's $190 to $175 billion, was an accounting change: it extended the assumed life of its data centres from 15 to 25 years, which lowers reported capex and spreads depreciation thinner. Second, committed spending that appears on no balance sheet yet is enormous: about $800 billion of leases signed but not commenced across the group by mid-year, $329 billion at Microsoft alone, with the lease payments typically servicing debt raised by the developers who build the sites. Third, the depreciation has barely started. Assets bought in 2026 hit the income statement in 2027 and 2028, and a 25-year life on a building does not change the four-to-six-year life of the servers inside it.

The honest summary: the revenue is proven, the return on the incremental dollar is not, and the capital to fund the gap is now raised from the public at prices set before the proof arrives.

THE ACCOUNTING OF A 25-YEAR LIFE

Microsoft's July decision to extend the assumed useful life of its data centres and office buildings from 15 to 25 years, effective at the start of fiscal 2027, cut its calendar-2026 reported capex guide from about $190 billion to about $175 billion without changing a single construction plan. The mechanism is lease accounting: longer lives, lower annual charges. The same change lowers depreciation in every future year. There is nothing improper in it; buildings do last. But the servers inside the buildings do not last 25 years, and the companies that have been quietly extending server lives since 2020 know it. When the reported cost of a build-out falls because of an assumption rather than a decision, the right response is not to adjust the model but to note that the model's inputs are now, in part, chosen by the people being modelled.

THE REVERSE OF PRIVATISATION

Six weeks ago I wrote about the privatisation of growth: companies financed and scaled in private markets, listing only after the growth has been captured by a closed circle of early investors. The AI build-out is the inverse. Growth is made public precisely when it costs cash, and the public is offered the bill rather than the harvest. SpaceX listed to fund an AI expansion that had produced no revenue; it raised $86 billion from the public and borrowed $25 billion eleven days later. Alphabet, Meta and Oracle, public for decades, reopened the primary market they had spent twenty years closing. The IPO pipeline of 2027 is not a list of companies that have finished growing. It is a list of companies that need to keep spending.

FIVE OBJECTIONS, ANSWERED

"Issuing equity at a high multiple is cheap capital; this is good capital allocation." It is cheap for the company and expensive for the holder if the return on the project falls short of the cost. The claim is only true after the fact, and the fact is three years away.

"Berkshire bought; that is the signal." Berkshire bought $10 billion at $351.81, a negotiated private placement, with an anchor's influence on terms. The public bought at $355.20 without it.

"These companies have $100 billion of cash each; they do not need the money." Alphabet had $126.8 billion at the end of the first quarter, Amazon $114.2 billion, Meta $82.5 billion. They raised anyway, because the cash covers one or two quarters of capex, not a multi-year plan, and because the rating agencies count gross debt.

"The depreciation life extension is standard." It may be. It is also a change that lowers this year's reported capex by $15 billion and next year's depreciation charge, made in the same quarter the market began to ask about returns.

"Capex is demand-driven; the backlogs prove it." They prove contracted revenue. They do not prove margin, and the largest single backlog, Microsoft's, was 45% one customer that loses money. A backlog is a promise from a buyer; capex is cash from the seller. The asymmetry is the whole question.

THE POLITICS ARRIVED THIS WEEK

One more variable entered the equation on 5 November. A day after Democrats won both chambers of Congress and governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, the AI complex lost about $3 trillion of value in a session. Forty-one local ballot measures to slow data-centre construction were decided on 3 November and most passed. The new governor of Texas, where about 27% of planned data-centre capacity sits, campaigned on an immediate moratorium. Ohio's governor-elect has proposed a conditional moratorium unless data centres pay 100% of their grid costs. The capital raised in June and October was raised on the assumption that the facilities could be built on schedule and that the grid would be paid for by someone else. Both assumptions now have a constituency against them. The equity holders of 2026 bought a promise; the voters of 2026 just added a condition to it.

WHO CAPTURES, WHO PAYS

The sellers of the shares capture certainty: capital raised now, at today's multiple, with no covenant and no maturity. Suppliers capture the capex, in cash, this year. Founders with dual-class structures, and from January a third class, capture control without funding it. Bondholders holding 2076 and 2126 paper capture a coupon and a very long wait.

The public, which includes every index fund and every pension, pays the price of the promise and holds the residual claim on whether it is kept. Existing shareholders pay in ownership: at Alphabet, the dilution from stock-based pay that buybacks used to cancel is now theirs to keep. Employees, paid in the same shares, discover that their compensation is funded by shareholder dilution rather than company cash. The bond market pays in duration, carrying 50- and 100-year claims on assets with five-year lives.

WHAT I WOULD MONITOR

Alphabet's fourth-quarter report in late January: whether buybacks resume, and how much of the remaining $27.6 billion of at-the-market capacity is used. Buybacks alongside continued issuance would be the strangest signal of all.

Meta's Class C distribution on 19 January and what follows. A non-voting share class is built to be sold. The first sale will show the price at which control-free Meta equity clears.

The pace of Oracle's $20 billion at-the-market programme and the next rating action. Oracle has the least margin for error and the most explicit dependence on equity to keep its rating.

Free cash flow at Alphabet, Amazon and Meta in the fourth and first quarters, against the 2027 capex guides due in late January and February. If the three stay negative while guiding higher, the equity raises of 2026 will not be the last.

The spread between Meta's and Oracle's bonds and the BBB index, and the 30-year Treasury. Widening means the bond market is closing; narrowing gives the companies room to stop selling shares.

The pricing of the AI listings of 2027, OpenAI and Anthropic among them, against what SpaceX did after its debut. If the next IPOs price below their last private rounds, the public market has started to set the price of the promise itself.

Whether the data-centre moratoria proposed in Texas and Ohio become law before the 2027 capex guides are given. If they do, a financing question becomes a permitting question, and the equity raised in 2026 funds capacity that cannot be built on time.

The criterion of success is measurable: free cash flow positive at the three largest builders while they hold their capex guidance, and buybacks resumed without new issuance. On that day the reversal of 2026 was a bridge. Until then it is the new model, and the model is this: the company that once paid you to leave is now charging you to stay.

If I were you, I would not sell on that. I would stop pretending I had not been told.
